[SUPER-APP CONTROL] Super-app best practice: (1) mini-app SDKs encourage moving real-time data handling (e.g. stock tickers, multiplayer sync) to Dedicated Workers; (2) container monitors enforce CPU usage caps on background workers (max 25% CPU core usage over 10s); (3) workers exceeding resource caps receive graceful termination signals.
standard_reference: W3C WebTransport Section 3 (WebTransport Interface & DedicatedWorkerGlobalScope Exposure)
relevance: Ensures fluid UI performance and stable frame rates during heavy real-time data streaming inside mini-apps.
operational_recommendation: Encourage worker-based WebTransport ingestion in developer guidelines and provide SDK starter templates.

title: W3C WebGPU establishes hardware-abstracted GPUAdapter and GPUDevice architectures with explicit limit contracts
summary: W3C WebGPU Candidate Recommendation defines GPUAdapter and GPUDevice interfaces with enforceable hardware limits on buffer, texture, and compute storage.
detail: [SPEC FACT] W3C WebGPU Candidate Recommendation provides direct, safe access to modern graphics and compute hardware (Vulkan, Metal, Direct3D 12): (1) Adapter and Device Split: `navigator.gpu.requestAdapter()` discovers available physical GPUs, while `adapter.requestDevice(descriptor)` creates an isolated logical device; (2) Hardware Limits Contract: the `GPUDevice.limits` interface exposes strict operational ceilings, including `maxBufferSize` (minimum default 256MB), `maxComputeWorkgroupStorageSize` (minimum default 16KB), and `maxTextureDimension2D` (minimum default 8192); (3) Sandboxed Execution: unlike legacy WebGL, WebGPU does not expose global state machines; all state is encapsulated in immutable pipeline and bind group objects; (4) Memory Isolation: GPU memory allocations are bound to the specific GPUDevice and cannot be accessed or inspected by cross-origin contexts. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Super-app container controls: (1) WebGPU access is gated by the mini-app manifest capability declaration (`"capabilities": ["gpu"]`); (2) the host container clamps `requiredLimits` to prevent rogue mini-apps from requesting excessive VRAM allocations on resource-constrained mobile devices; (3) low-tier devices (<3GB RAM) reject device creation or fall back to lightweight Canvas2D.
standard_reference: W3C WebGPU (Candidate Recommendation Draft) Sections 3-5
relevance: Enables next-generation 3D graphics and on-device AI/ML acceleration in super-app mini-apps under strict memory bounds.
operational_recommendation: Enforce container-level memory limit clamps during GPUDevice initialization based on device RAM tiers.

title: WebGPU Shading Language enforces compile-time memory safety, bounds checking and deterministic execution
summary: W3C WGSL eliminates arbitrary pointer arithmetic and mandates strict array/buffer out-of-bounds safety rules.
detail: [SPEC FACT] W3C WebGPU Shading Language (WGSL) Candidate Recommendation is designed specifically for web security and multi-platform compilation: (1) Memory Safety: WGSL prohibits raw pointer arithmetic and unchecked memory access; pointers only exist within specific address spaces (function, private, workgroup, storage, uniform); (2) Mandatory Bounds Checking: any out-of-bounds buffer or array read returns 0 or a clamped valid value; out-of-bounds writes are discarded without corrupting adjacent memory; (3) Deterministic Shader Validation: shader modules created via `device.createShaderModule()` undergo rigorous semantic and syntactic validation before compilation to native SPIR-V, MSL, or DXIL; (4) Driver Bug Mitigation: WebGPU implementations sanitize WGSL code to neutralize known GPU driver vulnerabilities and infinite execution hangs. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Security review and store policy: (1) static analysis during mini-app store submission parses WGSL shaders to detect abusive compute loops or cryptographic mining signatures; (2) host containers enforce maximum execution time limits on compute shaders; (3) non-compliant or unvalidated shader constructs trigger immediate build rejection.
standard_reference: W3C WebGPU Shading Language (WGSL) Candidate Recommendation Draft
relevance: Guarantees that mini-app shader code cannot crash native GPU drivers or execute out-of-bounds memory exploits.
operational_recommendation: Incorporate WGSL AST validation into automated store pipeline to flag crypto-mining and driver stress exploits.

title: WebGPU device.lost lifecycle arbitration enables resilient error recovery and background VRAM reclamation
summary: GPUDevice.lost Promise notifies applications of GPU context invalidation (OOM, driver reset, or deliberate host eviction) with reason tagging.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Under W3C WebGPU Section 5.3: (1) `device.lost` Promise: resolves with a `GPUDeviceLostInfo` object when the device is lost, carrying a `reason` property (`'destroyed'` for deliberate user/host disposal, or `'unknown'` for OS GPU driver reset, thermal throttling, or out-of-memory crash); (2) Non-Recoverable State: once a GPUDevice is lost, all associated buffers, textures, bind groups, and pipelines become invalid; subsequent commands result in silent no-ops or rejected promises; (3) Explicit Destruction: calling `device.destroy()` immediately releases GPU memory without waiting for garbage collection. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Host container lifecycle management: (1) when a mini-app enters background state, the super-app container issues `device.destroy()` to immediately reclaim VRAM for foreground tasks; (2) when the mini-app resumes, the container signals the guest runtime to re-initialize an adapter and rebuild GPU state; (3) mini-app SDK guidelines mandate listening to `device.lost` to ensure seamless user state restoration without crashing the super-app.
standard_reference: W3C WebGPU Section 5.3 (Device Loss & GPUDeviceLostInfo)
relevance: Prevents super-app out-of-memory crashes on mobile devices by systematically releasing GPU resources when mini-apps are backgrounded.
operational_recommendation: Call device.destroy() on backgrounded mini-apps; require mini-app developers to implement device.lost recovery handlers.

title: WebGPU timestamp queries enforce Cross-Origin Isolation gating and microsecond clock coarsening
summary: WebGPU restricts high-resolution timestamp queries behind Cross-Origin Isolation and applies clock coarsening to neutralize GPU cache timing attacks.
detail: [SPEC FACT] GPU execution timing can expose side-channel signals revealing cross-origin memory layouts or cryptographic keys: (1) Feature Gating: the `timestamp-query` feature in `requestDevice({ requiredFeatures: ['timestamp-query'] })` is restricted by browsers and user agents to secure contexts possessing Cross-Origin Isolation (`crossOriginIsolated = true`); (2) Clock Coarsening: even when permitted, timestamp query results are coarsened (e.g. rounded to 100 microseconds) to defeat microarchitectural cache-probing and side-channel timing attacks; (3) Disallowed Cross-Origin Textures: WebGPU canvas contexts cannot import tainted or cross-origin images without explicit CORS approval, preventing cross-origin pixel leakage through shader timing differentials. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Super-app security configuration: (1) mini-app containers disable `timestamp-query` by default; (2) only enterprise/certified partner mini-apps with strict COOP/COEP isolation can request performance profiling flags; (3) all external media assets imported into WebGPU textures must undergo strict origin verification.
standard_reference: W3C WebGPU Security Considerations (Timing Attacks & Timestamp Queries)
relevance: Protects against sophisticated GPU microarchitectural side-channel attacks across co-hosted mini-apps.
operational_recommendation: Disable timestamp-query feature flags in production mini-app containers; mandate CORS on all GPU texture assets.

title: Super-app container GPU governance establishes capability tiers, VRAM quotas and graceful WebGL 2 fallback
summary: Super-app multi-tier container governance audits WebGPU hardware availability, bounds VRAM usage per tenant, and arbitrates fallback to WebGL 2 or 2D rendering.
detail: [SPEC FACT] WebGPU support across mobile ecosystems remains heterogeneous (older Android devices and budget chipsets may lack Vulkan 1.1+ or stable drivers): (1) Capability Discovery: host containers evaluate `navigator.gpu` availability and driver stability profiles before exposing the API to mini-app WebViews; (2) Multi-Tier Fallback: standard mini-app rendering frameworks (Three.js, Babylon.js, PixiJS) support dual backends (WebGPU with WebGL 2 fallback); (3) Per-Tenant VRAM Quotas: host OS memory observers track aggregate GPU memory consumption per mini-app WebView process (alert at 150MB, hard kill at 300MB on mid-range devices); (4) Blacklisted GPU Drivers: super-app runtime maintains an up-to-date driver blocklist to disable WebGPU on devices known to suffer kernel panics or visual corruption. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Operating model: (1) include GPU capability tier in mini-app store discovery filters (hide WebGPU-only games from incompatible devices); (2) capture GPU crash telemetry via the host crash reporter; (3) automatically downgrade crashing mini-apps to WebGL 2 mode upon next launch.
standard_reference: W3C WebGPU Implementation Guidance & Chrome WebGPU Deployment Best Practices
relevance: Ensures wide compatibility, stability, and crash prevention across diverse smartphone hardware tiers in super-app deployments.
operational_recommendation: Implement client-side driver blocklists, device capability filtering in store search, and automatic WebGL 2 fallback.

title: W3C WebCodecs defines low-overhead hardware-accelerated video/audio encoding and decoding interfaces
summary: W3C WebCodecs Working Draft standardizes VideoEncoder, VideoDecoder, AudioEncoder, and AudioDecoder interfaces for raw frame manipulation without WebAssembly overhead.
detail: [SPEC FACT] W3C WebCodecs (Working Draft) exposes low-level access to the browser's built-in platform codecs (H.264, VP8, VP9, AV1, AAC, Opus): (1) Core Interfaces: provides `VideoDecoder`, `VideoEncoder`, `AudioDecoder`, and `AudioEncoder` operating on `VideoFrame`, `AudioData`, `EncodedVideoChunk`, and `EncodedAudioChunk` objects; (2) Hardware Acceleration: leverages native OS hardware decoders (Apple VideoToolbox, Android MediaCodec) without requiring bundled third-party WebAssembly codec binaries (saving 5-15MB bundle size and reducing battery consumption by 60-80%); (3) Real-Time Configuration: codecs support dynamic reconfiguration via `.configure()` (e.g. changing bitrate, latencyMode: 'realtime', or keyframe generation) without destroying the decoding session. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Container architecture: (1) super-app containers expose WebCodecs to approved mini-apps (video editors, security camera monitors, live-stream shopping); (2) enforce concurrent hardware decoder limits (maximum 2 simultaneous hardware decoders per mini-app) to avoid starving the host super-app; (3) automatically suspend decoder pipelines when mini-apps are minimized.
standard_reference: W3C WebCodecs (Working Draft) Sections 3-6
relevance: Enables ultra-fast, power-efficient multimedia editing and live video streams in mini-apps without bloating bundle size.
operational_recommendation: Expose WebCodecs for media-tier mini-apps; throttle concurrent hardware decoder allocations to prevent OS resource exhaustion.

title: WebCodecs VideoFrame lifecycle mandates explicit disposal to prevent GPU texture and memory leaks
summary: VideoFrame and AudioData objects hold underlying GPU memory and require explicit .close() invocations to avoid catastrophic memory leaks.
detail: [SPEC FACT] VideoFrame objects wrap native GPU surfaces (e.g. Android GraphicBuffer, Apple CVPixelBuffer, DirectX textures) or CPU shared memory: (1) Explicit Resource Disposal: because JavaScript garbage collection is non-deterministic and uncoupled from GPU memory pressure, VideoFrame instances MUST be explicitly released via `videoFrame.close()`; (2) Memory Leak Hazard: retaining unclosed VideoFrames in JavaScript arrays quickly exhausts GPU VRAM, leading to browser tab crashes within seconds during 60fps video processing (60 frames/sec * 8MB/frame = ~480MB/sec uncollected memory); (3) Transferable Semantics: VideoFrames can be cloned via `videoFrame.clone()` or transferred to Web Workers via `postMessage([frame], [frame])`, passing memory ownership and invalidating the source frame. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Mini-app container watchdog: (1) the container injects a proxy wrapper around `VideoDecoder` to monitor outstanding unclosed VideoFrame counts; (2) if unclosed frames exceed 30 frames, the container logs a memory warning and forces garbage collection; (3) store automated linter scans mini-app source code for missing `.close()` calls in decoder output callbacks.
standard_reference: W3C WebCodecs Section 7 (VideoFrame Interface & Resource Reclamation)
relevance: Eliminates the primary cause of out-of-memory crashes in video-processing mini-apps.
operational_recommendation: Enforce automated code inspection for VideoFrame.close() calls and track active frame counts in container telemetry.

title: W3C WebXR Device API standardizes spatial computing sessions, reference spaces and immersive rendering loops
summary: W3C WebXR Device API Recommendation defines XRSession modes ('inline', 'immersive-vr', 'immersive-ar') and XRReferenceSpace coordinates for spatial applications.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The W3C WebXR Device API Recommendation provides standardized hardware access to AR/VR headsets, smart glasses, and mobile AR camera tracking: (1) Session Modes: `navigator.xr.requestSession(mode)` supports `'inline'` (embedded canvas), `'immersive-vr'` (exclusive headset display), and `'immersive-ar'` (camera passthrough with virtual overlay); (2) Reference Spaces: applications request coordinate reference spaces (`'viewer'`, `'local'`, `'local-floor'`, `'bounded-floor'`, `'unbounded'`) to track user head position and movement relative to the physical room; (3) Render Loop: immersive sessions use `session.requestAnimationFrame(callback)` synchronized with the XR hardware refresh rate (72Hz, 90Hz, or 120Hz); (4) Input Sources: `session.inputSources` exposes controllers, optical hand-tracking joints, and screen-touch hit testing. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Container spatial governance: (1) mini-app AR experiences must declare `"capabilities": ["xr"]` in the mini-app manifest; (2) host container requires explicit user activation (transient user gesture) before invoking `requestSession()`; (3) super-app renders a permanent native close button / exit HUD over the immersive viewport to prevent rogue mini-apps from trapping users in VR/AR mode.
standard_reference: W3C WebXR Device API (Recommendation) Sections 3-7
relevance: Enables immersive AR product try-ons, 3D showroom mini-apps, and metaverse interactions within super-apps.
operational_recommendation: Mandate native overlay exit controls during immersive AR sessions and restrict session initialization to user gestures.

title: WebXR xr-spatial-tracking Permissions Policy restricts physical room scanning and biometric tracking telemetry
summary: The xr-spatial-tracking Permissions-Policy directive gates access to real-world coordinate tracking, protecting user physical environments and gaze data.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Spatial computing introduces severe privacy hazards (room dimension fingerprinting, biometric eye gaze tracking, facial expression inference): (1) Permissions Policy Directive: access to spatial tracking requires the `Permissions-Policy: xr-spatial-tracking=(self)` HTTP header or iframe `allow="xr-spatial-tracking"` attribute; without this directive, `navigator.xr.requestSession()` rejects with a `SecurityError`; (2) Raw Sensor Isolation: WebXR intentionally denies raw camera image access and raw depth sensor arrays to standard sessions; only derived pose matrices and hit-test results are exposed; (3) Gaze Privacy: eye tracking for foveated rendering is handled internally by the platform compositor and never exposed as raw gaze coordinates to script without specialized biometric permissions. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Privacy enforcement: (1) the super-app host controls the `xr-spatial-tracking` policy on mini-app container frames; (2) before granting AR/VR access, the host displays a native consent sheet explaining physical space access; (3) guest mini-apps are prohibited from transmitting spatial mesh data to third-party servers without explicit user disclosure and DPIA compliance.
standard_reference: W3C WebXR Device API Privacy & Security Considerations & Permissions Policy Directive
relevance: Protects user physical privacy and complies with EU GDPR and global privacy standards during AR/VR mini-app usage.
operational_recommendation: Enforce Permissions-Policy: xr-spatial-tracking gating and display clear host consent modals explaining spatial data handling.

title: Super-app container multimodal governance enforces camera, GPU and audio concurrency arbitration
summary: Unified host arbitration coordinates camera hardware, hardware media decoders, and audio focus between concurrent mini-apps and host features.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Multimodal mini-apps combine WebCodecs, WebXR, WebGPU, and camera capture simultaneously, placing extreme strain on mobile OS subsystems: (1) Hardware Mutex: mobile camera sensors (Camera2 on Android, AVCapture on iOS) cannot be shared simultaneously across multiple apps or disjoint WebViews; (2) Audio Session Arbitration: background music, voice chat, and audio decoders must adhere to OS audio focus protocols (e.g. ducking, pausing when incoming phone calls arrive); (3) Thermal Throttling: running WebGPU rendering alongside 4K WebCodecs decoding rapidly elevates device temperature, triggering OS-level CPU/GPU throttling down to 15-30fps. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Operating model: (1) the super-app native container acts as a central hardware arbiter, releasing camera and microphone locks immediately when a mini-app loses user focus; (2) host thermal observers monitor device battery temperature—if temperature exceeds 42°C, the container notifies the mini-app via a lifecycle event to reduce rendering resolution or frame rate; (3) mini-app review audits hardware utilization profiles to certify energy efficiency.
standard_reference: Super-App Container Practice: Multimodal Hardware Arbitration, Thermal Monitoring & Focus Lifecycle
relevance: Prevents device overheating, battery drain, and hardware lock contention in graphics- and media-heavy super-apps.
operational_recommendation: Implement container-level hardware mutexes for camera/mic and emit thermal warning events to throttling-capable mini-apps.

title: Chromium Multi-Process Architecture and Site Isolation enforce OS-level process boundaries for untrusted origins
summary: Site Isolation uses separate OS-level renderer processes for distinct web sites and hosts out-of-process iframes (OOPIF) to protect memory across origins.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Chromium Multi-Process Architecture and Site Isolation enforce rigid operating system process boundaries between mutually untrusted web origins: (1) Process Model: the browser maintains a privileged browser process, storage process, network service process, GPU process, and multiple sandboxed renderer processes; (2) Site Isolation & OOPIF: under Site Isolation, cross-site iframes are hosted in separate renderer processes via Out-of-Process iframes (OOPIF), ensuring that cross-origin HTML, DOM nodes, and JavaScript heaps never share the same address space; (3) Sandbox Hardening: renderer processes run with restricted OS tokens (Linux seccomp-bpf filters, Windows integrity levels, macOS sandboxing), denying raw filesystem, hardware, and inter-process access; (4) Side-Channel Immunity: memory isolation mitigates microarchitectural side-channel attacks (Spectre/Meltdown), preventing rogue script from reading memory across origins via high-resolution timing differentials. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Super-app container architecture: (1) configure WebView runtimes with strict process isolation per mini-app tenant; (2) ensure third-party embedded frames or advertisements inside mini-apps run in dedicated out-of-process renderer instances; (3) deny shared DOM or JavaScript execution contexts between distinct mini-app instances.
standard_reference: Chromium Process Model and Site Isolation Design Specification
relevance: Prevents cross-tenant data leaks and memory-scraping attacks in multi-mini-app super-app host environments.
operational_recommendation: Configure multi-process WebView flags and ensure cross-origin subframes run in isolated renderer processes.
superapp_applicability: Container: spawns isolated renderer processes per mini-app. Store: audits mini-app third-party iframe declarations. Runtime: isolates mini-app memory address spaces.

title: Android WebViewRenderProcessClient handles renderer process crashes, hangs and priority adjustments
summary: Android WebViewRenderProcessClient provides onRenderProcessGone and onRenderProcessUnresponsive callbacks to detect and handle out-of-process renderer crashes.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Android WebKit exposes `WebViewRenderProcessClient` to govern the out-of-process rendering pipeline: (1) Crash Handling: `onRenderProcessGone(WebView view, RenderProcessGoneDetail detail)` informs the host app when the renderer process has terminated; the `didCrash()` method distinguishes whether the renderer died due to an unhandled exception/signal or was terminated by the Android OS Low Memory Killer (LMK); (2) Unresponsive Recovery: `onRenderProcessUnresponsive(WebView view, WebViewRenderProcess renderer)` signals that the renderer UI thread is blocked by an infinite loop, heavy computation, or deadlock, enabling the host to terminate or reload the renderer; (3) Renderer Priority: `rendererPriorityAtExit()` indicates whether the process was running in high, medium, or low priority when killed; (4) Failure Isolation: returning `true` from `onRenderProcessGone` prevents the host super-app from crashing when a child renderer dies. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Super-app client resilience: (1) implement `WebViewRenderProcessClient` on all mini-app WebViews; (2) return `true` in `onRenderProcessGone` to trap the crash within the mini-app container without terminating the main super-app UI; (3) display an in-place reload/recovery prompt to the user and log crash telemetry with the exit reason to the monitoring pipeline.
standard_reference: Android WebView API: WebViewRenderProcessClient & RenderProcessGoneDetail
relevance: Ensures that a rogue or crashed mini-app cannot bring down the parent super-app application process on Android.
operational_recommendation: Register custom WebViewRenderProcessClient on all mini-app containers; intercept renderer crashes and provide graceful UI recovery.
superapp_applicability: Container: traps renderer crashes and recovers UI gracefully. Store: aggregates renderer crash rates to penalize unstable mini-apps. Runtime: captures exit reason and memory pressure diagnostics.

title: Apple WebKit WKProcessPool isolates web content processes and governs shared cookie/cache partitions
summary: WKProcessPool in WKWebViewConfiguration establishes isolated WebContent processes and governs cookie/storage partitions between distinct mini-apps on iOS.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Apple WebKit uses a multi-process architecture where web content executes in an out-of-process `com.apple.WebKit.WebContent` auxiliary process: (1) Process Pools: `WKProcessPool` represents an execution pool for WebContent processes; WebViews sharing the same `WKProcessPool` instance can share network connections, cookies, and cache pools, whereas WebViews assigned separate `WKProcessPool` instances run in strictly segregated processes with disjoint cache partitions; (2) Crash Notification: `WKNavigationDelegate.webViewWebContentProcessDidTerminate(_:)` is invoked when the underlying WebContent process terminates (e.g., Jetsam termination due to excessive RAM usage); (3) Configuration Binding: `WKWebViewConfiguration.processPool` must be configured at WebView initialization time and cannot be altered dynamically. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] iOS super-app container design: (1) allocate dedicated `WKProcessPool` instances for distinct mini-app tenants to enforce complete process and cache isolation; (2) implement `webViewWebContentProcessDidTerminate` to handle iOS Jetsam memory kills by reloading state or displaying a friendly restart sheet; (3) ensure the parent host process remains unaffected by WebContent termination.
standard_reference: Apple WebKit Documentation: WKProcessPool & WKWebViewConfiguration
relevance: Enforces complete process and storage segregation across independent mini-apps on iOS devices.
operational_recommendation: Maintain distinct WKProcessPool instances per mini-app tenant; implement webViewWebContentProcessDidTerminate to gracefully handle Jetsam memory kills.
superapp_applicability: Container: manages per-tenant WKProcessPool pools and traps WebContent crashes. Store: reviews memory usage limits for iOS mini-app certifications. Runtime: preserves user UI state across process recycles.

title: Renderer crash recovery requires transactional state snapshots and automated user session reconstruction
summary: Resilient super-app architectures persist incremental navigation checkpoints to restore user state seamlessly after unexpected renderer process termination.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Renderer crashes are an unavoidable reality on mobile devices due to aggressive OS Low Memory Killers (Android LMK, iOS Jetsam) and unhandled GPU/memory errors: (1) State Volatility: when a renderer process terminates, all volatile in-memory JavaScript heap state, active DOM nodes, and unsaved form inputs are permanently lost; (2) State Checkpointing: resilient web platforms implement continuous or transactional checkpointing, serializing active route parameters, scroll offsets, and draft inputs into persistent storage (IndexedDB or host-mediated native SQLite); (3) Safe Re-hydration: upon renderer relaunch following a crash, the host container restores the saved snapshot after verifying the checkpoint integrity. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Super-app crash recovery standards: (1) container SDK provides an automated state-save hook (`onSaveMiniAppState`) called before backgrounding and periodically during navigation; (2) after a renderer crash, the host presents a contextual banner ('Mini-app recovered') with a single-tap restore action; (3) if repeated crashes occur within 60 seconds (crash loop), the container disables auto-restore and prompts the user to launch with a fresh cache.
standard_reference: Super-App Container Resilience Standard: Automated State Checkpointing & Crash Loop Prevention
relevance: Prevents user frustration and data loss during mobile background memory reclamation and unexpected mini-app crashes.
operational_recommendation: Implement automatic mini-app state snapshotting and circuit-breaker crash loop protection in the container SDK.
superapp_applicability: Container: captures state snapshots and restores navigation stacks after crash. Store: monitors crash recovery success ratios. Runtime: triggers periodic checkpoint persistence.

title: Super-App Multi-Process Topology decouples UI Host, Native Service Broker, and Sandboxed Mini-App Renderers
summary: A 3-tier multi-process architecture isolates the Host UI process, Background Service Broker, and Sandboxed Mini-App Renderer processes via IPC.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Enterprise super-apps (e.g. WeChat, Alipay) operate a multi-process architecture to balance security, performance, and memory utilization: (1) Host Main Process: manages super-app shell UI, bottom navigation tabs, and system lifecycle; (2) Background Service Process: hosts long-running network synchronization, push gateway connections, and offline download managers, immune to UI thread jank; (3) Sandboxed Mini-App Renderer Processes: each active mini-app runs in a dedicated secondary process (e.g. `:appbrand0`, `:appbrand1`), isolated from the host process via Android IPC (Binder/AIDL) or iOS XPC; (4) Process Recycling: the super-app maintains a warm pool of pre-warmed, blank renderer processes (1-2 standby instances) to achieve instant sub-200ms mini-app launch times. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Operating rules: (1) bind IPC communication with strict permission capability tokens, ensuring renderer processes cannot invoke privileged host methods directly; (2) enforce an LRU process reclamation policy that kills inactive background mini-app processes when system RAM drops below threshold; (3) pre-warm standby renderer processes only when battery level is above 20% and device is not in power-saving mode.
standard_reference: Super-App Multi-Process Architecture Best Practices & Android Process Model
relevance: Delivers sub-200ms instant startup while safeguarding the super-app against memory exhaustion and UI freezing.
operational_recommendation: Adopt a 3-tier process model (Host UI, Service Broker, Isolated Renderers) with pre-warmed standby renderer pools.
superapp_applicability: Container: manages Android/iOS multi-process lifecycle and Binder/XPC bridges. Store: audits IPC bridge interface boundaries. Runtime: executes guest code strictly inside sandboxed renderer processes.

title: RFC 3284 VCDIFF standardizes byte-level differential encoding for bandwidth-efficient software updates
summary: RFC 3284 specifies the VCDIFF generic differential and linear-time compression data format utilizing ADD, COPY, and RUN instructions.
detail: [SPEC FACT] RFC 3284 defines VCDIFF, a compact, byte-oriented differential compression format for delta updates: (1) Encoding Instructions: VCDIFF encodes changes between a source dictionary and target data using three primary operations: ADD (insert new data), COPY (copy bytes from source or previous target window), and RUN (repeat a single byte); (2) Address Encoding: leverages compact variable-length integer encoding and relative address caches to minimize instruction overhead; (3) Secondary Compression: supports chaining with secondary compressors (such as Deflate or Zstandard) to achieve optimal compression ratios; (4) Deterministic Reconstruction: delta decoding runs in linear time and deterministic memory, making it ideal for mobile devices with constrained compute and memory. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Super-app distribution engine: (1) when a publisher releases a minor mini-app update, the build pipeline computes a VCDIFF delta relative to the previous version; (2) delta packages average 80-95% smaller than full packages (reducing typical 4MB bundles to 200-400KB); (3) clients download the delta package over cellular networks, drastically lowering bandwidth costs and reducing update latency.
standard_reference: IETF RFC 3284: The VCDIFF Generic Differential and Linear-Time Data Compression Format
relevance: Enables micro-sized over-the-air mini-app updates, reducing download latency and mobile data consumption.
operational_recommendation: Implement RFC 3284 VCDIFF delta generation in the release packaging pipeline for consecutive mini-app versions.
superapp_applicability: Container: applies VCDIFF delta patches against cached base packages. Store: generates and stores version-to-version delta artifacts. Runtime: verifies base package checksum before applying delta.

title: RFC 8878 Zstandard provides real-time decompression speeds and domain-specific custom dictionary compression
summary: RFC 8878 specifies Zstandard (zstd) combining Finite State Entropy (FSE) and custom dictionary training for high-ratio, fast-decompression payloads.
detail: [SPEC FACT] RFC 8878 specifies Zstandard (zstd), a modern compression algorithm engineered for ultra-fast real-time decompression: (1) Entropy Encoding: combines Finite State Entropy (FSE, an asymmetric numeral system) with Huffman coding to achieve superior compression ratios and multi-gigabyte/sec decompression throughput; (2) Custom Dictionary Training: zstd supports training domain-specific custom dictionaries from representative sample sets, dramatically improving compression efficiency on small payloads (such as JSON configs, HTML templates, and JS scripts); (3) Framing & Integrity: the zstd framing format incorporates optional Content_Checksum (xxHash-64) fields to verify uncompressed payload integrity directly during streaming decompression; (4) Multi-Level Tuning: offers 22 compression levels, allowing offline servers to compress at maximum level (19-22) while mobile clients decompress at near-memory-bus bandwidth. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Mini-app asset compression standard: (1) train a global super-app mini-app dictionary containing common framework headers, API tokens, and standard CSS rules; (2) compress all mini-app code chunks using zstd with the shared dictionary; (3) leverage streaming zstd decompression in native container loaders to eliminate launch bottlenecks.
standard_reference: IETF RFC 8878: Zstandard Compression and The application/zstd Media Type
relevance: Maximizes payload compression ratios and accelerates on-device decompression for instant mini-app startup.
operational_recommendation: Standardize zstd compression with pre-trained shared framework dictionaries across the mini-app distribution CDN.
superapp_applicability: Container: integrates native zstd decompressor with shared dictionary support. Store: trains and distributes versioned framework dictionaries. Runtime: verifies xxHash-64 payload checksums.

title: Super-App Differential Packaging builds directed delta update graphs between consecutive active versions
summary: Differential update pipelines generate delta packages across an N-version compatibility window and bind patch artifacts to base SHA-256 hashes.
detail: [SPEC FACT] In mature super-app ecosystems (e.g. WeChat, Alipay), package delivery is managed through a directed version graph: (1) Version Graph: for any newly approved release V(n), the store packaging service automatically generates delta patches against the top active deployed versions (V(n-1), V(n-2), V(n-3)); (2) Cryptographic Binding: each delta package header explicitly encodes `base_package_hash` (SHA-256) and `target_package_hash` (SHA-256), ensuring patches can only be applied to bit-identical source files; (3) Manifest Negotiation: when a client requests an update via API, it sends its currently installed `package_hash`; if a matching delta exists, the CDN returns the lightweight delta patch; otherwise, it falls back to the full standalone archive. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Platform engineering controls: (1) delta generation pipeline triggers automatically upon release promotion; (2) restrict delta depth to 3 preceding minor versions to manage CDN storage overhead; (3) require all delta packages to be signed by the platform release authority.
standard_reference: Super-App Package Engineering: Version-Graph Delta Synthesis & Checksum Validation
relevance: Minimizes network transfer size for 90%+ of returning users while maintaining robust fallback paths.
operational_recommendation: Generate delta patches for the last 3 active versions during automated release staging and bind to base package SHA-256 hashes.
superapp_applicability: Container: negotiates delta updates via client hash headers. Store: publishes version delta graphs and manifests. Runtime: executes patch verification and assembly.

title: Atomic patch reconstruction enforces pre-validation, staged assembly and automatic fallback to full archives
summary: Client-side patch reconstruction verifies base hash before patching, validates target hash post-patching, and falls back to full archives on mismatch.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Safe OTA delta patching requires strict transactional staging to prevent corrupting local application state: (1) Pre-Patch Verification: the client verifies that the locally installed base package matches the delta header's `base_package_hash`; if local corruption or tampering is detected, the patch operation aborts immediately; (2) Staged Assembly: the patch is applied in an isolated temporary directory (`tmp/patch_staging/`), never modifying the live running mini-app directory directly; (3) Post-Patch Validation: the newly assembled package is hashed (SHA-256) and compared against `target_package_hash`; only if the hash matches exactly is the staging directory atomically swapped (via atomic filesystem rename) to become the active release; (4) Automatic Full-Download Fallback: if patch download, decompression, or hash verification fails at any stage, the container discards the staged files and transparently downloads the full baseline package. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Container reliability policies: (1) prohibit running mini-apps while their active directory is being updated (swap occurs between sessions or at launch time); (2) log patch failure telemetry to track corrupted base package occurrences across device models; (3) purge staging artifacts if free disk space is under 100MB.
standard_reference: Container Reliability Guide: Atomic Patch Assembly, Digest Verification & Rollback Fallback
relevance: Eliminates mini-app corruption, launch crashes, and bricked client states caused by corrupted or partial delta updates.
operational_recommendation: Enforce strict pre-patch hash check, staging directory assembly, post-patch hash match, and automatic full package download fallback.
superapp_applicability: Container: manages staging directories and atomic directory swaps. Store: provides canonical package hashes in update manifests. Runtime: recovers gracefully from patch application failures.

title: Apple App Store Rule 4.7 governs OTA updates, prohibiting native binary execution and mandating audit logs
summary: Apple App Store Review Guideline 4.7 permits dynamic code delivery solely for interpreted web technologies while strictly forbidding native binary execution.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Apple App Store Review Guidelines Section 4.7 (Mini-Apps, Mini-Games, Streaming Games, Chatbots, Plug-ins) strictly regulates dynamic code and asset delivery: (1) Interpreted Code Only: dynamic code delivered over-the-air must be interpreted (HTML5, CSS, JavaScript, WebAssembly) and cannot execute native machine binaries or bypass system sandboxes; (2) Host Policy Compliance: mini-apps offered within the host app must comply with all App Store Review Guidelines, including privacy protections, user safety, and in-app purchase rules; (3) Indexing & Logging: the host app must maintain an up-to-date index of all mini-apps and software offered through its service and make software available for Apple review upon request; (4) Emergency Killswitch: the host must possess the technical capability to immediately revoke or remove any non-compliant or malicious mini-app from all client devices. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Compliance governance for super-app operators: (1) ensure all OTA updates contain only web assets (JS, CSS, images, Wasm) and strictly prohibit native dynamic libraries (.so, .dylib); (2) audit all mini-app OTA updates through the store console before publishing; (3) implement immediate remote package revocation API (`revokePackage(appId, version)`) to satisfy App Store compliance mandates.
standard_reference: Apple App Store Review Guidelines §4.7 (Design: Mini-Apps, Mini-Games, Streaming Games)
relevance: Ensures the super-app maintains full regulatory compliance and avoids App Store rejection or ejection when distributing OTA mini-apps.
operational_recommendation: Enforce strict static analysis to block native binaries in mini-app OTA packages; maintain full audit logs and remote killswitch mechanisms.
superapp_applicability: Container: blocks native library loading and enforces remote takedown commands. Store: maintains mini-app index and review records for platform compliance. Runtime: executes only sandboxed web code.

title: W3C Trace Context Recommendation standardizes distributed traceparent headers across heterogeneous systems
summary: W3C Trace Context defines the traceparent HTTP header format (version-trace_id-parent_id-trace_flags) for end-to-end distributed transaction tracing.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The W3C Trace Context Recommendation specifies standardized HTTP headers for correlating distributed trace events across decoupled microservices and client applications: (1) `traceparent` Header: formatted as a 4-part hyphen-separated string: `version-trace_id-parent_id-trace_flags` (e.g. `00-4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736-00f067aa0ba902b7-01`); (2) Trace ID: a globally unique 16-byte (32 hex character) identifier representing the entire distributed transaction; (3) Parent ID / Span ID: an 8-byte (16 hex character) identifier representing the caller's specific request span; (4) Trace Flags: an 8-bit field where bit 0 (`01`) indicates whether the trace was sampled for detailed recording; (5) `tracestate`: conveys vendor-specific trace identification routing across multiple observability systems without mutating the standard traceparent. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Super-app tracing implementation: (1) native container generates a unique W3C `traceparent` upon every mini-app launch and user interaction flow; (2) automatically injects `traceparent` into all outgoing fetch/XHR requests made by the mini-app to its backend; (3) passes `traceparent` across the native JSAPI bridge to correlate client WebView events with native host background services.
standard_reference: W3C Trace Context Recommendation §2 & §3 (traceparent & tracestate)
relevance: Provides the foundational distributed tracing standard to link mini-app client actions with backend super-app services.
operational_recommendation: Inject standardized W3C traceparent headers across all mini-app network requests and native bridge invocations.
superapp_applicability: Container: generates trace IDs and propagates traceparent across bridge interfaces. Store: provides distributed tracing correlation dashboards for developers. Runtime: injects trace headers into outgoing HTTP traffic.

title: W3C Baggage defines open contextual key-value propagation for distributed application telemetry
summary: W3C Baggage establishes the 'baggage' HTTP header format to transport user context, tenant IDs, and telemetry metadata across service boundaries.
detail: [SPEC FACT] W3C Baggage Candidate Recommendation establishes a standard mechanism to transport contextual key-value pairs across distributed trace paths: (1) `baggage` Header: contains a comma-separated list of key-value pairs (`key=value;property=value`) representing application-level metadata (e.g. `userId=u123,appId=miniapp-456,tenant=enterprise`); (2) Decoupled Context: unlike trace identifiers, baggage values are intended for business context, tenant attribution, and dynamic routing rather than span identification; (3) Propagation Contract: intermediaries and services inspect, modify, or append entries to baggage and forward the updated header to downstream dependencies; (4) Quota Constraints: specifications recommend capping baggage header size (typically max 8KB or 64 entries) to avoid HTTP header overflow. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Super-app context governance: (1) container injects immutable baggage attributes (`miniapp_id`, `miniapp_version`, `host_version`, `device_tier`) into outgoing mini-app requests; (2) backend gateway uses baggage to route requests to appropriate tenant service clusters and rate-limiting buckets; (3) sanitizes baggage headers to prevent mini-apps from spoofing system-level claims.
standard_reference: W3C Baggage Candidate Recommendation §2 (baggage header syntax and propagation)
relevance: Enables seamless tenant attribution, routing, and contextual observability across distributed super-app systems.
operational_recommendation: Inject standardized W3C baggage headers containing verified mini-app metadata while enforcing strict size and mutation controls.
superapp_applicability: Container: injects verified app identity and device context into baggage headers. Store: leverages baggage tags for tenant-level operational analytics. Runtime: sanitizes incoming and outgoing baggage pairs.

title: OpenTelemetry Distributed Tracing API bridges asynchronous JSAPI calls and native host execution
summary: OpenTelemetry Trace API and Context Propagators inject and extract distributed trace context across JavaScript WebViews and native mobile host runtimes.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The OpenTelemetry (OTel) Trace API standardizes span creation, lifecycle management, and in-process context propagation: (1) Tracer and Spans: a `Tracer` creates `Span` objects representing individual units of work, capturing start/end timestamps, span status (OK, Error), span kind (Client, Server, Internal), and structured attributes; (2) Context Propagators: the OTel Propagator API (`inject` and `extract`) serializes the active `Context` into carrier objects (HTTP headers, JSON IPC payloads) and reconstructs it in remote or cross-language runtimes; (3) Cross-Boundary Tracing: when a mini-app calls a native JSAPI bridge (e.g. `my.pay` or `wx.getLocation`), the client tracer injects the active context into the bridge message; the native host SDK extracts the context and creates a child span (`native.jsapi.execution`), achieving unbroken end-to-end visibility. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Super-app observability integration: (1) bundle a lightweight OpenTelemetry JavaScript SDK within the mini-app runtime environment; (2) automatically wrap all native bridge calls with OpenTelemetry spans; (3) stream span batches asynchronously to the super-app telemetry collector via low-priority background channels.
standard_reference: OpenTelemetry Trace API Specification & Context Propagators API Specification
relevance: Provides end-to-end tracing across the JavaScript-to-Native bridge, pinpointing latency bottlenecks in JSAPI execution.
operational_recommendation: Implement OpenTelemetry context injection and extraction across the native JSAPI bridge interface.
superapp_applicability: Container: extracts bridge trace context and links native execution spans. Store: provides latency heatmaps and bridge bottleneck analytics. Runtime: wraps JSAPI client calls in OpenTelemetry spans.

title: End-to-End Super-App Tracing correlates client user interactions, native bridge calls, gateway hops, and microservices
summary: Unified distributed tracing captures the complete journey from user UI interaction through native bridge, API gateway, and backend microservice spans.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Modern super-app transactions span complex multi-tier architectures encompassing mobile UI, native OS bridges, edge API gateways, and backend microservices: (1) Client Span: user taps 'Checkout' -> generates client span `miniapp.checkout.click`; (2) Bridge Span: client calls `container.requestPayment()` -> creates child span `native.bridge.payment_prompt`; (3) Gateway Span: native code dispatches payment intent to super-app gateway -> gateway receives request, validates VAPID/JWT, creates server span `gateway.payment.authorize`; (4) Downstream Microservices: gateway calls core banking and merchant settlement services -> creates nested spans `ledger.reserve_balance` and `settlement.create_invoice`; (5) Unified Trace ID: the initial 16-byte `trace_id` is propagated through every hop, linking frontend rendering latency, native bridge overhead, network transport, and database query durations into a single cohesive trace tree. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Platform engineering controls: (1) enforce trace propagation standards across all partner mini-app gateways; (2) configure adaptive sampling (sample 100% of errors and high-latency transactions, 1% of successful transactions) to balance telemetry fidelity against backend ingestion costs; (3) expose trace search tools to developers to debug cross-tier failures.
standard_reference: Super-App End-to-End Distributed Tracing Topology & Microservice Correlation Guide
relevance: Enables rapid root-cause isolation for transaction failures, bridge timeouts, and network slowdowns across all ecosystem tiers.
operational_recommendation: Mandate end-to-end trace correlation using W3C Trace Context across client, bridge, gateway, and backend service tiers.
superapp_applicability: Container: propagates unified trace IDs across network and IPC boundaries. Store: delivers end-to-end trace visualization in developer consoles. Runtime: links user gestures to backend transaction traces.

title: Distributed telemetry mandates automated PII scrubbing, token redaction, and strict data minimization
summary: Telemetry pipelines must scrub personally identifiable information (PII), credentials, and sensitive headers from trace attributes and baggage before storage.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Distributed tracing headers and telemetry spans are prone to accidental exfiltration of sensitive user data, violating GDPR, CCPA, and enterprise privacy regulations: (1) High-Risk Vectors: URL query strings containing session tokens, `Authorization` headers, passwords, credit card numbers, national identity numbers, and biometric coordinates; (2) Data Minimization: GDPR Article 5(1)(c) mandates that telemetry data collection be strictly adequate, relevant, and limited to what is necessary in relation to the purposes for which they are processed; (3) Automated Scrubbing: OpenTelemetry Collector and client SDK pipelines utilize regex-based redaction processors to sanitize attribute values before export; (4) Non-PII Baggage: baggage headers must never transport raw customer identities, plain-text email addresses, or unencrypted phone numbers. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Super-app privacy standards: (1) container telemetry agent scrubs all URL query parameters matching known token/credential patterns (`token`, `auth`, `password`, `key`, `secret`); (2) span attributes automatically mask payment account numbers (retain only last 4 digits); (3) prohibit mini-app developers from attaching custom PII attributes to public telemetry spans; (4) run automated CI/CD linter checks on telemetry instrumentation to detect unscrubbed logging.
standard_reference: OWASP API Security Top 10 & OpenTelemetry Privacy and Data Scrubbing Guidelines
relevance: Guarantees that distributed observability pipelines comply with global data protection laws and do not leak user secrets.
operational_recommendation: Deploy automated PII scrubbing and regex token redaction within client telemetry SDKs and server collectors.
superapp_applicability: Container: redacts sensitive parameters from outgoing spans and baggage. Store: verifies privacy compliance of developer telemetry configs. Runtime: blocks logging of raw credentials or payment tokens.

title: W3C Clear-Site-Data HTTP Response Header specifies authoritative origin-bound data sanitization
summary: W3C Clear-Site-Data specification standardizes an HTTP response header that instructs user agents to clear cache, cookies, DOM storage, and execution contexts for an origin.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The W3C Clear-Site-Data specification (and living draft at w3c.github.io/webappsec-clear-site-data/) defines an imperative HTTP response header sent by servers to instruct user agents to wipe locally stored data associated with the response origin. The header syntax accepts comma-separated quoted string tokens: (1) `"cache"`: instructs the client to flush network caches, prerendered pages, script caches, and WebGL shader caches; (2) `"cookies"`: clears cookies, HTTP basic/digest authentication credentials, and origin-bound tokens; (3) `"storage"`: clears all DOM storage mechanisms including `localStorage`, `sessionStorage`, IndexedDB databases, WebSQL, and Service Worker registrations; (4) `"executionContexts"`: neuters and reloads all active browsing contexts currently rendering documents from the origin; (5) `"*"`: wildcard directive clearing all categories simultaneously. User agents MUST only accept and process Clear-Site-Data delivered over an authenticated, secure HTTPS connection and MUST NOT process the header when served by a service worker synthetic response. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Super-app security integration: (1) mini-app API gateways inject `Clear-Site-Data: "*"` on sensitive credential invalidation and explicit logout endpoints; (2) container network interceptors inspect HTTP response headers and coordinate local native cache purging whenever this header is received.
standard_reference: W3C Clear-Site-Data Specification §3.1 & §4.2 (Header Field & Clear Algorithms)
relevance: Provides the web standard foundation for origin-bound storage clearing across WebViews and mini-app runtimes.
operational_recommendation: Enforce HTTPS-only delivery of Clear-Site-Data headers and integrate container network handlers to trigger native WebView cache invalidation.
superapp_applicability: Container: parses Clear-Site-Data on intercepted responses and initiates WebView storage eviction. Store: validates mini-app logout configurations during automated review. Runtime: terminates active execution contexts and resets in-memory script state.

title: Mini-App lifecycle storage clearing triggers govern session termination, account switching, and package deprecation
summary: Super-app containers trigger systematic storage purges across distinct lifecycle milestones: explicit logout, user switching, uninstallation, and emergency deprecation.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Enterprise data governance and privacy frameworks mandate that client-side data must not persist indefinitely across distinct user sessions or after application termination: (1) User Logout: upon user sign-out from either the host super-app or individual mini-app, session tokens, cached profile data, and transient DOM storage must be purged to prevent session fixation and unauthorized access; (2) Account Switching: when a user switches accounts on a shared device, the container must isolate or wipe the previous account's local storage partitions to prevent cross-account data leakage; (3) Mini-App Uninstallation: when a user removes a mini-app from their favorites or installed list, the container must delete all dedicated directory trees, IndexedDB databases, and cached assets; (4) Security Incident Purge: upon discovery of a compromised mini-app version or vulnerable package, the super-app platform pushes a forced-eviction command that wipes local data across all active client instances. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Super-app container controls: (1) native container registers a lifecycle hook `onMiniAppTerminated` or `onMiniAppUninstalled` that invokes native storage eviction routines; (2) platform operator console supports targeted remote wipe commands targeted at specific mini-app IDs.
standard_reference: Super-App Container Storage Lifecycle Governance & Incident Response Architecture
relevance: Ensures user privacy and eliminates residual authentication artifacts across multi-tenant super-app containers.
operational_recommendation: Implement automated storage cleanup hooks tied to account switching, app deletion, and platform remote wipe signals.
superapp_applicability: Container: executes complete partition directory unlinking upon app removal. Store: exposes emergency remote data wipe commands in operator incident consoles. Runtime: listens for session termination signals and flushes memory stores.

title: Native container WebView storage eviction APIs coordinate iOS WKWebsiteDataStore and Android WebStorage/CookieManager
summary: Native super-app shells employ platform-specific WebView storage APIs to programmatically evict cookies, cache, WebSQL, and IndexedDB without clearing entire host app data.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Mobile operating systems provide granular APIs to inspect and evict WebView storage data without affecting the native host application's private keychain or settings: (1) Apple WebKit (`WKWebsiteDataStore` & `WKWebsiteDataRecord`): iOS developers use `[WKWebsiteDataStore defaultDataStore]` or custom non-persistent data stores. To evict data for a specific mini-app origin, the container queries `fetchDataRecordsOfTypes:completionHandler:` passing `WKWebsiteDataTypeCookies`, `WKWebsiteDataTypeDiskCache`, `WKWebsiteDataTypeMemoryCache`, `WKWebsiteDataTypeOfflineWebApplicationCache`, `WKWebsiteDataTypeLocalStorage`, `WKWebsiteDataTypeIndexedDBDatabases`, and `WKWebsiteDataTypeWebSQLDatabases`, followed by `removeDataOfTypes:forDataRecords:completionHandler:`; (2) Android WebView (`WebStorage` & `CookieManager`): Android native shells utilize `WebStorage.getInstance().deleteOrigin(origin)` to remove WebSQL and LocalStorage, `CookieManager.getInstance().removeAllCookies(ValueCallback)` or per-URL cookie deletion, and `WebView.clearCache(true)` to purge disk and RAM caches. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Container architecture: (1) wrap iOS and Android native storage eviction APIs in a unified cross-platform interface `MiniAppStorageManager.purgeOrigin(origin, mask)`; (2) execute asynchronous data eviction off the main UI thread to prevent UI freezing during large IndexedDB removals.
standard_reference: Apple WebKit WKWebsiteDataStore API & Android WebView WebStorage Architecture
relevance: Provides concrete native platform implementations for isolating and wiping mini-app WebView storage.
operational_recommendation: Encapsulate WKWebsiteDataStore and WebStorage into a unified native container storage management module.
superapp_applicability: Container: manages per-origin storage tracking and invokes platform eviction methods. Store: documents storage cleanup guarantees for third-party compliance. Runtime: requests graceful storage flushes prior to container teardown.

title: OWASP MASVS-STORAGE and HTML5 Security guidelines mandate client storage token elimination and residual protection
summary: OWASP Mobile Application Security Verification Standard (MASVS-STORAGE) and HTML5 Security Cheat Sheet mandate that sensitive tokens must not persist in unencrypted Web Storage.
detail: [SPEC FACT] OWASP security standards provide comprehensive controls for client-side storage security in hybrid and mobile environments: (1) OWASP MASVS-STORAGE: requires that sensitive data (passwords, private API keys, payment tokens, unmasked PII) is never stored in unencrypted client-side files or standard WebView storage; requires that cached data is sanitized upon session termination and that backup configurations exclude sensitive application directories; (2) OWASP HTML5 Security Cheat Sheet: warns that `localStorage` and `sessionStorage` are completely accessible to any JavaScript running within the origin, making them vulnerable to DOM XSS extraction; advises against storing bearer authentication tokens or session IDs in Web Storage, recommending HttpOnly secure cookies or in-memory closures instead; (3) Residual Data Defense: temporary files, image caches, and unencrypted SQLite/IndexedDB records must be actively shredded or overwritten when deleted to prevent forensic recovery on rooted or compromised devices. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Platform security controls: (1) static analysis scanner inspects mini-app bundles for hardcoded calls storing tokens in `localStorage.setItem('token', ...)`; (2) container provides a secure encrypted key-value JSAPI (`my.setStorage` backed by hardware-backed Keystore/Keyring) for any data requiring client persistence.
standard_reference: OWASP MASVS v2.0 (MASVS-STORAGE) & OWASP HTML5 Security Cheat Sheet
relevance: Defines baseline security requirements preventing sensitive data leakage in mini-app client storage.
operational_recommendation: Prohibit storing bearer tokens in unencrypted Web Storage and offer container-mediated encrypted storage APIs.
superapp_applicability: Container: provides AES-GCM encrypted storage JSAPIs backed by platform keystores. Store: runs automated linter checks blocking plain-text credential persistence. Runtime: blocks insecure storage of session secrets.

title: Super-App container storage quota enforcement and LRU eviction policies protect host disk health
summary: Super-app containers enforce strict per-mini-app storage ceilings (e.g. 10MB-50MB) and execute Least-Recently-Used (LRU) cache eviction to maintain host system stability.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Unrestricted client-side caching in multi-tenant super-app containers risks exhausting device flash storage, triggering OS low-memory warnings, and degrading host performance: (1) Storage Quota Ceilings: leading super-app platforms (WeChat, Alipay, Baidu Smart Programs) enforce hard storage limits on mini-apps: WeChat limits synchronous local storage to 10MB per mini-app and aggregate storage across all mini-apps to 50MB; (2) Quota Exceeded Exceptions: when a mini-app attempts to exceed its allocated quota, the storage API returns a standardized error code (e.g. `storage:fail quota exceeded`), preventing further writes while preserving existing data; (3) Least-Recently-Used (LRU) Cache Eviction: when the super-app's global mini-app cache reaches a designated threshold (e.g. 500MB or 85% device capacity), an automated LRU background engine identifies inactive mini-apps and deletes their package caches and transient files while retaining user configuration state. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Container storage policy matrix: (1) tiered quotas: Tier 1 (Standard) = 10MB, Tier 2 (Media/Game) = 50MB with explicit entitlement declaration; (2) continuous disk monitoring with proactive LRU cleanup during app idle states.
standard_reference: Super-App Multi-Tenant Storage Quota & LRU Eviction Architecture Specification
relevance: Maintains host device performance and prevents rogue mini-apps from consuming excessive device storage.
operational_recommendation: Enforce explicit per-app storage quotas with standardized failure handling and automated LRU background cache reclamation.
superapp_applicability: Container: tracks storage consumption per mini-app origin and applies LRU eviction algorithms. Store: reviews storage tier upgrade requests during submission. Runtime: emits quota warnings when usage crosses 80% threshold.

title: PrivacyCG Storage Access API specifies explicit permission lifecycle for unpartitioned state in embedded contexts
summary: PrivacyCG Storage Access API defines document.hasStorageAccess() and document.requestStorageAccess() methods allowing embedded frames to request unpartitioned cookie access.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The Privacy Community Group (PrivacyCG) Storage Access API (SAA) specification establishes a standardized mechanism for cross-origin embedded contexts (iframes) to query and request access to their first-party (unpartitioned) storage under strict privacy constraints: (1) `document.hasStorageAccess()`: returns a Promise resolving to a boolean indicating whether the calling context already possesses access to its unpartitioned state; (2) `document.requestStorageAccess()`: initiates an explicit permission request to unlock first-party cookies; (3) User Interaction Requirement: the API requires transient user activation (`UserActivation.isActive` via touch or click) before `requestStorageAccess()` can be invoked, preventing silent background probing; (4) Permissions Policy Integration: iframe containers must include `allow="storage-access"` in their iframe attributes to authorize access; (5) User Prompting & Heuristics: user agents evaluate security heuristics (prior top-level user visits) and may prompt the user before granting unpartitioned access. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Super-app container policy: (1) host container configures WebView settings to enforce storage access delegation; (2) third-party partner widgets embedded inside mini-apps must utilize SAA rather than relying on legacy unpartitioned third-party cookie sharing.
standard_reference: PrivacyCG Storage Access API Specification §3 & §5 (Methods & Security Considerations)
relevance: Provides the web standard pattern for controlled access to cross-site identity and storage within embedded mini-app contexts.
operational_recommendation: Require embedded third-party frames within mini-apps to implement Storage Access API flows backed by explicit user gestures.
superapp_applicability: Container: arbitrates storage access permission grants between mini-app host and embedded iframes. Store: scans embedded frame declarations for proper Permissions Policy tags. Runtime: mediates requestStorageAccess calls.

title: PrivacyCG Extending Storage Access API enables scoped unpartitioned localStorage, sessionStorage, and IndexedDB
summary: PrivacyCG proposal extends Storage Access API beyond cookies to enable embedded frames to obtain unpartitioned access to localStorage, IndexedDB, and CacheStorage.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The PrivacyCG specification 'Extending Storage Access API (SAA) to non-cookie storage' addresses the limitation where standard SAA only unblocks cookies, leaving non-cookie web storage partitioned: (1) Non-Cookie Storage Handles: provides API extensions (`window.storageAccess` or options dictionary `requestStorageAccess({all: true})`) enabling access to first-party `localStorage`, `sessionStorage`, `indexedDB`, and `caches`; (2) Origin Storage Binding: once granted, the returned storage handle binds directly to the embedded origin's top-level unpartitioned datastore rather than the partitioned context; (3) Cross-Context Isolation: access remains strictly bound to the requesting frame and does not automatically leak to other cross-origin frames; (4) Ephemeral Lifetime: non-cookie storage access expires when the document unloads or when the session context is closed. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Super-app architecture: (1) allows authorized partner mini-apps to access their shared enterprise IndexedDB schemas when loaded inside authorized host aggregator portals; (2) enforces strict tenant origin validation to prevent unauthorized sub-frames from intercepting enterprise offline data.
standard_reference: PrivacyCG Extending Storage Access API to non-cookie storage §2 & §3
relevance: Enables complex mini-app components (rich editors, offline carts, payment SDKs) to synchronize non-cookie storage cleanly.
operational_recommendation: Support non-cookie storage handles in container WebViews to allow authorized partner widgets to access shared IndexedDB stores.
superapp_applicability: Container: exposes extended storage handles across WebView partitions. Store: reviews declared non-cookie storage access scopes during approval. Runtime: isolates non-cookie storage access per requesting frame origin.

title: PrivacyCG requestStorageAccessFor API empowers top-level hosts to proactively request storage access for embedded origins
summary: PrivacyCG requestStorageAccessFor() API allows top-level pages to request unpartitioned storage access on behalf of embedded origins prior to rendering.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The PrivacyCG `requestStorageAccessFor` specification addresses user experience friction by allowing a top-level site to proactively request unpartitioned storage access on behalf of a specific cross-site resource origin: (1) Method Signature: `document.requestStorageAccessFor(requestedOrigin)` called by the top-level document; (2) Proactive Granting: allows the parent page to establish storage access before embedded iframes or image resources load, eliminating jarring layout shifts and redundant child-frame prompts; (3) Top-Level User Gesture: requires user activation on the top-level document; (4) Origin Scoping: access is strictly constrained to the declared `requestedOrigin` and does not grant blanket third-party access; (5) First-Party Sets / Related Website Sets Integration: browsers may grant access automatically without prompts if the top-level site and requested origin belong to the same verified enterprise administrative entity. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Super-app orchestration: (1) super-app parent shell calls `requestStorageAccessFor(partnerOrigin)` when navigating the user into a recognized co-branded mini-app flow; (2) verifies partner origin authenticity against the super-app manifest allowlist before issuing the request.
standard_reference: PrivacyCG requestStorageAccessFor API Specification §2 & §4
relevance: Provides a smooth, prompt-free UX for verified enterprise partner mini-apps integrated within the super-app shell.
operational_recommendation: Utilize requestStorageAccessFor for verified partner origins to eliminate nested user consent prompts while maintaining origin isolation.
superapp_applicability: Container: executes top-level storage access authorization for verified partner origins. Store: maintains the allowlist of verified partner domain origins. Runtime: passes storage tokens to authorized embedded partner views.

title: IETF CHIPS Cookies Having Independent Partitioned State isolates embedded state via top-level partition double-keying
summary: IETF CHIPS (draft-cutler-httpbis-partitioned-cookies) introduces the 'Partitioned' cookie attribute, double-keying cookies by top-level site and embedded origin.
detail: [SPEC FACT] IETF Internet-Draft `draft-cutler-httpbis-partitioned-cookies` (Cookies Having Independent Partitioned State - CHIPS) standardizes partitioned cookies to preserve third-party subresource functionality while eliminating cross-site tracking: (1) `Partitioned` Attribute: servers declare partitioned cookies by appending the `Partitioned` directive in the `Set-Cookie` header (e.g. `Set-Cookie: __Host-id=123; Secure; Path=/; SameSite=None; Partitioned;`); (2) Partition Key: partitioned cookies are keyed using a 2-tuple: `{top-level site, cookie partition key}` rather than just the cookie's host domain; (3) Privacy Guarantees: if mini-app A and mini-app B both embed widget C (`service.example`), widget C receives two distinct, isolated cookie jars that cannot be correlated to track the user across mini-apps; (4) Secure Prefix Requirement: partitioned cookies must include the `__Host-` prefix or declare `Secure; SameSite=None;`, guaranteeing end-to-end cryptographic transit. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Super-app backend architecture: (1) configure all shared service endpoints to issue `Partitioned` cookies for embedded mini-app resources; (2) container network layer verifies double-keyed partition isolation across different mini-app tenants.
standard_reference: IETF Internet-Draft draft-cutler-httpbis-partitioned-cookies §3 & §5
relevance: Enables embedded mini-app services (maps, payment widgets, analytics) to maintain state without enabling cross-app tracking.
operational_recommendation: Mandate the Partitioned attribute on all cookies issued by embedded third-party services in mini-apps.
superapp_applicability: Container: enforces partition-key routing for WebView cookie jars. Store: verifies third-party cookie configurations during app submission. Runtime: segregates embedded cookie caches by top-level mini-app ID.

title: Super-App partner widget storage partitioning policy isolates multi-tenant mini-app embedded components
summary: Super-app multi-tenant containers enforce complete storage partitioning across embedded widgets, allowing selective cross-origin state federation only via signed bridge tokens.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Modern super-apps host complex ecosystems where third-party mini-apps frequently embed components from external vendors (payment gateways, loyalty systems, logistics trackers, chat widgets): (1) Default Storage Partitioning: all client-side storage (localStorage, IndexedDB, cookies) allocated to an embedded component is strictly partitioned by the host mini-app ID and widget origin; (2) Prohibition of Covert Storage Channels: components are blocked from using shared native caches, shared file descriptors, or undocumented OS pasteboards to exchange persistent tracking identifiers; (3) Controlled State Federation: when cross-widget state exchange is legitimately required (e.g. sharing user loyalty status with a merchant mini-app), data must be mediated through the super-app native bridge using cryptographically signed, short-lived, single-use federation tokens; (4) Auditability: container logs all cross-context data transfers for compliance verification under data protection regulations (GDPR/PDPA). [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Super-app governance matrix: (1) automated WebView sandbox policies partition storage by default; (2) bridge APIs reject cross-app storage sharing unless explicitly declared in the app manifest and approved by security review.
standard_reference: Super-App Multi-Tenant Storage Partitioning & Third-Party Component Isolation Policy
relevance: Guarantees enterprise-grade tenant privacy and prevents cross-app data leakage across heterogeneous third-party mini-apps.
operational_recommendation: Enforce double-keyed storage partitioning across all embedded mini-app components and mediate data federation through signed JSAPIs.
superapp_applicability: Container: isolates WebView storage stores per mini-app instance. Store: audits embedded widget permissions and declared storage access. Runtime: monitors cross-context communication channels for unauthorized data leakage.

title: WHATWG HTML BroadcastChannel API specifies low-overhead same-origin pub-sub message dispatching
summary: WHATWG HTML Living Standard BroadcastChannel API enables windows, iframes, and Web Workers of the same origin to broadcast messages across browsing contexts.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The WHATWG HTML Living Standard (§9.4 Channel messaging and BroadcastChannel interface) specifies the `BroadcastChannel` API for lightweight publish-subscribe communication across same-origin execution environments: (1) Interface Definition: `const channel = new BroadcastChannel(channelName);` constructs a channel bound strictly to the calling context's origin; (2) Pub-Sub Contract: `channel.postMessage(message)` broadcasts serialized data to all active `BroadcastChannel` instances listening on `channelName` within the same origin, excluding the sender itself; (3) Event Handling: listening contexts receive events via `channel.onmessage = (event) => { ... }` or `addEventListener('message', ...)`; (4) Origin Isolation Boundary: channels with identical names instantiated in different origins are completely isolated and cannot communicate; (5) Resource Cleanup: invoking `channel.close()` cleanly unbinds the channel from the browser event loop, preventing memory leaks in long-running applications. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Container integration: (1) native container allows mini-apps to leverage BroadcastChannel for cross-page navigation synchronization; (2) container runtime tracks active channel counts to prevent unbounded subscription resource consumption.
standard_reference: WHATWG HTML Living Standard §9.4 (BroadcastChannel interface)
relevance: Provides the web standard baseline for seamless client-side state synchronization across multi-page mini-app architectures.
operational_recommendation: Standardize BroadcastChannel usage for intra-mini-app multi-view event dispatching and enforce channel closure in unmount hooks.
superapp_applicability: Container: respects origin isolation boundaries for native-backed WebView messaging. Store: validates channel usage in mini-app code reviews. Runtime: facilitates low-latency pub-sub event passing between active views.

title: WHATWG Structured Clone Algorithm enforces secure deep serialization and object transfer semantics
summary: WHATWG HTML Living Standard Structured Clone Algorithm serializes complex object graphs while stripping prototypes and handling transferable objects safely.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The WHATWG HTML Living Standard (§2.7 Safe passing of structured data / StructuredSerialize and StructuredDeserialize) defines the Structured Clone Algorithm governing message serialization across BroadcastChannel, MessagePort, and Worker boundaries: (1) Supported Types: safely copies complex cyclic object graphs, Arrays, Maps, Sets, Date, RegExp, Blob, File, ArrayBuffer, and TypedArrays; (2) Prototype Stripping: objects cloned via structured clone lose their prototype chain and methods (functions, DOM nodes, Error stack details in certain contexts), preventing Prototype Pollution attacks across boundaries; (3) Transferable Objects: supports memory ownership transfer for `ArrayBuffer`, `MessagePort`, and `ImageBitmap` via `structuredClone(value, { transfer: [buffer] })`, detaching the buffer from the sender context and transferring zero-copy memory to the receiver; (4) Native Global Method: modern runtimes expose `window.structuredClone(value)` for deterministic deep-copy operations. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Super-app security controls: (1) all JSAPI bridge payloads passing between mini-app WebViews and native host code are validated through structured clone semantics; (2) prohibits passing executable closures or function pointers across the native container boundary.
standard_reference: WHATWG HTML Living Standard §2.7 (Safe passing of structured data)
relevance: Prevents code execution vulnerabilities and prototype pollution across mini-app execution contexts and bridge layers.
operational_recommendation: Enforce structured clone serialization across all inter-context messages and bridge IPC layers, rejecting non-transferable functions.
superapp_applicability: Container: validates message payloads across IPC boundaries using structured clone rules. Store: lints code for insecure prototype mutations. Runtime: provides native structuredClone implementation for mini-app scripts.

title: WHATWG Web Storage StorageEvent coordinates cross-window synchronization upon storage mutations
summary: WHATWG Web Storage specification defines the StorageEvent interface fired on sibling window contexts whenever localStorage is mutated.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The WHATWG HTML Web Storage specification (§11 Web storage) standardizes the `StorageEvent` mechanism for notifying other browsing contexts of same-origin storage modifications: (1) Event Trigger: fired on `window` whenever `localStorage.setItem()`, `localStorage.removeItem()`, or `localStorage.clear()` is called from another document within the same origin; (2) Event Properties: includes `key` (mutated key name), `oldValue` (previous value), `newValue` (updated value), `url` (URL of document that executed the change), and `storageArea` (reference to localStorage object); (3) Execution Scope: the event is intentionally NOT fired in the document that made the mutation, eliminating infinite echo loops; (4) Synchronous Commit Semantics: while event firing is asynchronous across contexts, storage writes commit synchronously to the underlying origin partition. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Super-app coordination pattern: (1) multi-window mini-apps (e.g. tablet split-view or dual-screen displays) utilize `StorageEvent` listeners to automatically synchronize local state updates; (2) container native storage wrappers mirror StorageEvents across independent WebView processes.
standard_reference: WHATWG HTML Living Standard §11.2 (The StorageEvent interface)
relevance: Enables responsive, declarative state synchronization across concurrent mini-app windows without polling.
operational_recommendation: Implement StorageEvent listeners for reactive cross-window data synchronization and sanitize event payload parsing.
superapp_applicability: Container: relays storage mutation events between multi-instance WebViews. Store: provides guidelines for multi-window state management. Runtime: dispatches standard StorageEvents upon local data changes.

title: Multi-instance mini-app state synchronization architecture coordinates shopping carts, auth tokens, and global logout
summary: Super-app multi-instance architectures coordinate distributed client state—shopping carts, token refreshes, and logout signals—across parallel views.
