detail: [SPEC FACT] Modern super-apps support multi-instance execution where a mini-app may have multiple active views (e.g. product detail view, floating chat overlay, embedded checkout drawer, background service worker): (1) Shopping Cart Replication: adding an item to the cart in a browsing tab immediately broadcasts an event via BroadcastChannel, updating the floating cart badge in real time; (2) Session Token Refresh: when a background API call refreshes an expired access token, the new token is broadcast to all active views, preventing redundant authentication calls and race conditions; (3) Cross-Tab Logout Coordination: if the user signs out in one view, an authenticated `LOGOUT` broadcast notifies all sibling instances to immediately clear their in-memory state and redirect to the login screen; (4) State Conflict Resolution: implementations adopt Last-Write-Wins (LWW) or vector clocks to resolve concurrent state mutations across decoupled views. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Platform engineering standards: (1) mini-app container SDK provides a pre-configured `StateSyncManager` encapsulating BroadcastChannel with automatic fallback to StorageEvent; (2) audits mini-app state handlers to ensure sensitive data is not broadcast across unsecured public channels.
standard_reference: Super-App Multi-Instance State Synchronization & Distributed Cart Architecture
relevance: Eliminates stale data anomalies and ensures consistent user experiences across multi-page mini-app sessions.
operational_recommendation: Deploy a container-level StateSyncManager SDK to standardize cart replication, token refresh, and logout broadcasts.
superapp_applicability: Container: facilitates intra-app state broadcast routing across separate WebView instances. Store: verifies state synchronization patterns during technical review. Runtime: provides client helper libraries for reactive state binding.

title: Super-App event bus governance enforces message size caps, namespace isolation, and burst rate limiting
summary: Container-mediated event bus infrastructure enforces strict message payload limits (e.g. 64KB), channel namespacing, and rate limiting to prevent DoS attacks.
detail: [SPEC FACT] High-throughput event channels in multi-tenant environments introduce risks of resource exhaustion, thread starvation, and cross-tenant interference if left ungoverned: (1) Message Size Caps: container enforces a maximum payload size (typically 64KB per message) on inter-context broadcasts; attempts to send oversized payloads throw a `MessageSizeExceededError`, requiring developers to store large binary blobs in IndexedDB/OPFS and broadcast lightweight reference URIs instead; (2) Channel Namespace Isolation: native container prefixes all channel names with the calling mini-app's unique ID (`miniapp_${appId}_${channelName}`) at the IPC boundary, guaranteeing that two independent mini-apps cannot accidentally or maliciously collide or eavesdrop on channels; (3) Rate Limiting and Burst Throttling: container throttles message dispatching to a maximum sustained rate (e.g. 100 messages/sec with burst allowance of 200), preventing runaway loops from locking the browser thread; (4) Diagnostic Monitoring: telemetry tracks dropped messages and abnormal message volumes. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Super-app container controls: (1) native message dispatcher enforces quota policing and automatic payload validation; (2) terminates or suspends rogue mini-apps that repeatedly trigger rate-limit violations.
standard_reference: Super-App Container Event Bus Governance & Inter-Context Throttling Specification
relevance: Guarantees runtime performance, prevents denial-of-service loops, and secures inter-context communications.
operational_recommendation: Enforce automated namespace prefixing, 64KB payload caps, and burst rate-limiting across all container event buses.
superapp_applicability: Container: prefixes channel namespaces and applies rate-limiting filters on bridge events. Store: flags excessive event publishing during automated static analysis. Runtime: throws standardized errors when payload quotas are exceeded.

title: W3C Long Tasks API 1.0 establishes the 50ms UI thread execution threshold for jank detection
summary: W3C Long Tasks API 1.0 defines PerformanceLongTaskTiming reporting any continuous UI thread execution exceeding 50ms to prevent unresponsive interactions.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The W3C Long Tasks API 1.0 specification defines `PerformanceLongTaskTiming` extending `PerformanceEntry` to identify tasks that monopolize the UI thread: (1) 50ms Threshold: Any discrete task execution lasting longer than 50 milliseconds is reported as a long task, grounded in the RAIL model threshold where 50ms tasks ensure 100ms response latency to user input; (2) PerformanceObserver Integration: Registered via `const observer = new PerformanceObserver((list) => { ... }); observer.observe({ entryTypes: ['longtask'] });`; (3) TaskAttributionTiming: Each long task entry contains an `attribution` array exposing `name` (e.g. 'script', 'layout'), `entryType` ('taskattribution'), `startTime`, `duration`, `containerType` ('iframe', 'embed', 'object'), `containerName`, `containerId`, and `containerSrc`; (4) Culprit Context Scoping: Identifies whether the jank originated within the top-level browsing context or a nested cross-origin iframe. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Container telemetry controls: (1) Super-app WebView runtime automatically injects a longtask observer upon container initialization; (2) Aggregates Total Blocking Time (TBT) during mini-app launch lifecycle, triggering telemetry warnings if cumulative long tasks exceed 300ms before First Meaningful Paint.
standard_reference: W3C Long Tasks API 1.0 (W3C Working Group Note / Draft)
relevance: Provides the foundational browser standard for detecting main-thread monopolies and UI freezes in web runtimes.
operational_recommendation: Deploy container-level PerformanceObserver for longtask entries and enforce a strict 50ms task budget on all mini-app lifecycle hooks.
superapp_applicability: Container: monitors main thread blocking time during WebView execution. Store: audits developer task execution profiles during certification. Runtime: provides native hooks to intercept long tasks.

title: PerformanceLongAnimationFrameTiming (LoAF) provides fine-grained animation frame bottleneck breakdown
summary: PerformanceLongAnimationFrameTiming (LoAF) observes animation frames exceeding 50ms, detailing blockingDuration, renderDuration, and styleAndLayoutDuration.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The Long Animation Frames (LoAF) web standard (specified in Chromium/Blink and MDN PerformanceLongAnimationFrameTiming) supersedes classic long tasks by contextualizing jank within the browser rendering pipeline: (1) Observation Interface: Subscribed via `observer.observe({ type: 'long-animation-frame', buffered: true })`; (2) Rendering Phase Timers: Exposes exact millisecond breakdowns for `renderDuration` (total frame rendering time), `styleAndLayoutDuration` (recalc style, layout, pre-paint passes), and `blockingDuration` (total time tasks on the main thread blocked other work within the frame); (3) Frame Cadence Metrics: Exposes `desiredExecutionStart` (when requestAnimationFrame or render steps were intended to execute) and `duration` (total elapsed frame time from first task to frame presentation); (4) Scripts Attribution Collection: Contains a `scripts` property returning an array of `PerformanceScriptTiming` objects identifying the exact offending JS executions. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Super-app rendering governance: (1) Host container evaluates LoAF entries across mini-app views to separate JavaScript computational bottlenecks from excessive DOM/CSS style reflows; (2) Automatically throttles non-essential background animations when `blockingDuration` exceeds 100ms in active views.
standard_reference: Long Animation Frame Timing Specification & MDN PerformanceLongAnimationFrameTiming API
relevance: Delivers granular visibility into frame drops, rendering jank, and style calculation bottlenecks.
operational_recommendation: Ingest LoAF telemetry into super-app APM dashboards to pinpoint whether jank is caused by JS CPU execution or CSS reflow complexity.
superapp_applicability: Container: captures LoAF metrics directly from Blink/WebKit rendering pipelines. Store: sets acceptable LoAF thresholds (<5% frame drop rate) in store SLA. Runtime: exposes LoAF telemetry to mini-app devtools.

title: PerformanceScriptTiming isolates exact invoker functions, source URLs, and execution positions
summary: PerformanceScriptTiming pinpoints offending scripts with invoker, invokerType, sourceURL, sourceFunctionName, and sourceCharPosition.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The `PerformanceScriptTiming` interface (exposed via `PerformanceLongAnimationFrameTiming.scripts`) provides granular, deterministic script attribution for long tasks: (1) Invoker Attribution: `invoker` string identifies the initiator (e.g. 'button.onclick', 'Promise.then', 'setTimeout', 'FetchEvent'); (2) Invoker Type Categorization: `invokerType` classifies the trigger into 'user-callback', 'event-listener', 'promise-resolve', 'render-request', or 'classic-script'; (3) Source Code Resolution: `sourceURL` specifies the exact script file URI, `sourceFunctionName` indicates the executed function identifier, and `sourceCharPosition` pinpoints the character offset in the source file; (4) Execution vs Pause Metrics: Exposes `executionDuration` (active CPU execution time) alongside `pauseDuration` (synchronous blocking time inside `alert()`, synchronous XHR, or blocking modal dialogs). [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Super-app developer governance: (1) Mini-app crash and jank reporting gateways parse `PerformanceScriptTiming` objects and automatically map source URLs/character positions to developer source maps; (2) Automatically flags third-party analytics/ad SDK scripts that trigger jank without blaming the primary mini-app business logic.
standard_reference: PerformanceScriptTiming Interface Specification (W3C / Web Performance WG)
relevance: Enables automated, line-level root cause diagnosis of UI blocking code across complex mini-app bundles.
operational_recommendation: Require automated source-map symbolication of PerformanceScriptTiming telemetry in super-app developer consoles.
superapp_applicability: Container: extracts script timing attribution metadata from native WebViews. Store: provides automated performance diagnostics reports to developers upon submission. Runtime: isolates third-party SDK script impact.

title: Interaction to Next Paint (INP) root cause attribution correlates input delay, processing time, and presentation delay
summary: Super-app responsiveness monitoring decomposes INP into input delay, processing time, and presentation delay using LoAF and Event Timing APIs.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Interaction to Next Paint (INP) measures overall page responsiveness by tracking the latency of all discrete click, tap, and keyboard interactions throughout the user lifecycle: (1) Three Phase Latency Decomposition: Total interaction latency is partitioned into `Input Delay` (time waiting for main thread idle to begin processing), `Processing Duration` (time executing event handlers, callbacks, and microtasks), and `Presentation Delay` (time taken by the browser compositor to recalculate style, layout, paint, and display the next frame); (2) Event Timing API Bridge: Correlating `PerformanceEventTiming` entries with concurrent `PerformanceLongAnimationFrameTiming` entries reveals whether high INP is caused by queued background tasks (input delay) or expensive UI mutations (presentation delay); (3) Good Responsiveness Baseline: Core Web Vitals standard requires 75th percentile INP under 200 milliseconds. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Platform engineering controls: (1) Super-app container SDK embeds an INP watchdog that captures full LoAF traces for any interaction exceeding 200ms; (2) Surfaces real-user interaction latency distributions in the mini-app store developer portal.
standard_reference: W3C Event Timing API & Core Web Vitals INP Measurement Architecture
relevance: Guarantees fluid touch interaction across super-app mini-apps on diverse mid-tier and low-tier mobile devices.
operational_recommendation: Establish a mandatory 200ms 75th-percentile INP gate in super-app performance monitoring and auto-generate LoAF breakdown reports.
superapp_applicability: Container: calculates interaction phases across native touch events and WebView dispatch. Store: displays INP compliance badges in the store catalog. Runtime: instruments event listeners with timing probes.

title: Super-app container telemetry enforces automated watchdog demotion and background script throttling
summary: Container-level watchdog infrastructure enforces sub-50ms task budgets, throttles unresponsive mini-apps, and logs ANR telemetry.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Uncontrolled JavaScript execution on mobile devices causes Application Not Responding (ANR) dialogs, thermal throttling, and battery drain: (1) Watchdog Polling Interval: Native container maintains a background watchdog thread pulsing the WebView main thread every 500ms; if the main thread fails to respond within 3000ms, the watchdog captures a thread stack trace; (2) Background Demotion & Throttling: When a mini-app is navigated away from or minimized, the container automatically invokes `freeze()` or demotes its timer frequency (clamping `setTimeout`/`setInterval` to >=1000ms and pausing requestAnimationFrame), freeing CPU cycles for the host; (3) Telemetry Aggregation: Client SDK samples 1% of LoAF and longtask events, batching JSON payloads to the super-app APM endpoint with network backpressure adaptation; (4) Quota Enforcement: Mini-apps exhibiting persistent >500ms freezes have their catalog ranking downgraded or are blocked from featured store placement. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Container enforcement mechanisms: (1) Native watchdog forces process termination if a mini-app locks the main thread for >5000ms; (2) Restores host super-app UI gracefully without crashing the parent application.
standard_reference: Super-App Container Watchdog & Resource Throttling Governance Standard
relevance: Protects host super-app stability and device battery life against rogue, unoptimized mini-app scripts.
operational_recommendation: Implement container watchdog stack-sampling for 3s UI freezes and clamp background timers to >=1000ms upon mini-app minimization.
superapp_applicability: Container: enforces timer clamping and process isolation during background transitions. Store: penalizes unresponsive apps in catalog search algorithms. Runtime: provides graceful UI recovery overlays.

title: WHATWG Declarative Shadow DOM specifies zero-JS streaming shadow tree hydration via template shadowrootmode
summary: WHATWG HTML Living Standard standardizes Declarative Shadow DOM using <template shadowrootmode> to parse shadow roots directly from HTML without script execution.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The WHATWG HTML Living Standard (§4.12.3 The template element / Declarative Shadow DOM) standardizes native declarative shadow tree parsing directly in HTML: (1) Markup Syntax: An author specifies `<template shadowrootmode="open|closed" shadowrootclonable shadowrootdelegatesfocus>`; the HTML parser immediately attaches a `ShadowRoot` to the parent element and consumes the template contents into the shadow tree during initial HTML parsing; (2) Zero-JS SSR Rendering: Eliminates client-side JavaScript execution previously required to call `element.attachShadow({ mode: 'open' })`, completely avoiding Flash of Unstyled Content (FOUC) during server-side rendered (SSR) or streaming responses; (3) Clonable Shadow Roots: The `shadowrootclonable` attribute allows shadow roots created declaratively to be cloned via `Node.cloneNode(true)`, enabling repeated UI component templating; (4) Focus Delegation: `shadowrootdelegatesfocus` automatically forwards focus to the first focusable child inside the shadow tree when clicked. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Container rendering optimization: (1) Super-app mini-app pre-compiler serializes page UI trees into DSD chunks, allowing native WebView engines to render complete encapsulated UI components before main-thread JavaScript bundles finish executing; (2) Decreases First Contentful Paint (FCP) by 30-50% on low-end mobile devices.
standard_reference: WHATWG HTML Living Standard §4.12.3 (The template element and Declarative Shadow DOM)
relevance: Enables ultra-fast server/worker streaming of encapsulated UI widgets without client-side hydration delays.
operational_recommendation: Adopt Declarative Shadow DOM templates in mini-app compile targets to achieve immediate, non-blocking component rendering.
superapp_applicability: Container: renders DSD templates during initial WebView byte-stream parsing. Store: verifies template syntax conformance in mini-app package linter. Runtime: bypasses imperative attachShadow calls for SSR pages.

title: WHATWG Custom Elements lifecycle callbacks standardize deterministic containment and attribute reactivity
summary: WHATWG Custom Elements specification defines connectedCallback, disconnectedCallback, and attributeChangedCallback for robust component encapsulation.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The WHATWG HTML Living Standard (§4.13 Custom elements) standardizes the autonomous custom element lifecycle contracts: (1) Deterministic Callbacks: Defines `connectedCallback()` (invoked when element is appended to document DOM), `disconnectedCallback()` (invoked when removed, enabling mandatory teardown of observers and event listeners), `adoptedCallback()` (invoked when moved to a new document), and `attributeChangedCallback(name, oldValue, newValue)` (invoked upon declared attribute modifications); (2) Reactive Attribute Observation: Component registers `static get observedAttributes()` array; the engine triggers synchronous callbacks only for observed keys, minimizing overhead; (3) Shadow DOM Binding: Integrates natively with `this.attachShadow()` or Declarative Shadow DOM attached roots; (4) Custom Element Registry: Defined via `customElements.define('mini-widget', MiniWidgetClass)`. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Mini-App SDK component containment: (1) Super-app UI component libraries (buttons, navbars, carousel, payment cards) are packaged as custom elements; (2) Native container enforces mandatory resource disposal inside `disconnectedCallback` to prevent memory leaks across mini-app page transitions.
standard_reference: WHATWG HTML Living Standard §4.13 (Custom elements)
relevance: Provides the vendor-neutral web standard foundation for modular, reusable mini-app UI components.
operational_recommendation: Mandate custom element encapsulation for mini-app SDK standard widgets with strict unmount cleanup in disconnectedCallback.
superapp_applicability: Container: registers platform-provided custom elements into the mini-app runtime environment. Store: audits custom element namespacing to avoid tag collisions. Runtime: orchestrates deterministic component lifecycle.

title: CSS Shadow Parts specifies controlled styling boundaries via ::part() and exportparts without cascade pollution
summary: CSS Shadow Parts (W3C Working Group Note / Draft) standardizes the ::part() pseudo-element to expose explicit styling hooks across shadow boundaries.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The CSS Shadow Parts specification defines the `::part()` pseudo-element and `exportparts` attribute to balance strict encapsulation with design-system themability: (1) Controlled Exposure: Elements inside a shadow root tag specific DOM nodes with `part="label icon"`; outside CSS can style these elements via `custom-button::part(label) { color: blue; }` while all unexposed shadow DOM nodes remain strictly encapsulated and impervious to external CSS selectors; (2) Nested Shadow Forwarding: The `exportparts` attribute forwards inner shadow parts through intermediate custom elements (e.g. `exportparts="icon: button-icon"`), creating cleanly documented multi-tier UI abstractions; (3) Cascade Protection: Eliminates CSS conflicts, global specificity wars, and accidental style bleeding between the super-app host environment and third-party mini-app widgets. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Super-app design system governance: (1) Host container provides official theme packs (light/dark mode, brand palettes) that target mini-app SDK components exclusively through standardized `::part()` interfaces; (2) Prohibits third-party mini-apps from attempting deep shadow piercing, ensuring host UI security.
standard_reference: CSS Shadow Parts (W3C Candidate Recommendation Draft)
relevance: Solves the fundamental tension between strict style isolation and global branding/theming in super-app mini-apps.
operational_recommendation: Design all super-app platform UI components with explicit part attributes and exportparts mappings for theme customization.
superapp_applicability: Container: applies host theme tokens dynamically to exposed mini-app component parts. Store: verifies that mini-apps do not use deprecated shadow piercing selectors. Runtime: maintains impervious style encapsulation.

title: Mini-app dual-thread rendering leverages Worker DSD template generation for sub-100ms FCP
summary: Super-app dual-thread architecture generates Declarative Shadow DOM strings in the background Worker thread, streaming them to the WebView renderer.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Mainstream super-app runtimes (WeChat, Alipay, WindVane) enforce a dual-thread architecture separating the View Layer (WebView UI thread) from the Service Layer (Web Worker/V8 JavaScript logic thread): (1) Architectural Bottleneck: Historically, the worker thread computed virtual DOM diffs and serialized JSON patches over native IPC bridges, resulting in high serialization latency and main-thread layout thrashing; (2) DSD Streaming Pipeline: With Declarative Shadow DOM, the worker thread compiles page templates directly into DSD HTML markup strings containing `<template shadowrootmode="open">`; (3) Zero-Bridge IPC Pipe: The native container streams this markup directly into the WebView's document stream or parses it via `element.setHTMLUnsafe(chunk)` / `DOMParser`; (4) Instant Hydration: The browser engine renders CSS and HTML layouts natively in parallel without waiting for JavaScript frameworks to hydrate the DOM. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Super-app container framework optimization: (1) Container runtime implements a streaming pipe between JavaScript Worker and WebView renderer; (2) Reduces initial page launch First Contentful Paint (FCP) from ~400ms down to <100ms on mid-tier mobile hardware.
standard_reference: Super-App Dual-Thread Architecture & Declarative Template Streaming Standard
relevance: Dramatically optimizes startup latency by eliminating client-side VDOM reconciliation on the main UI thread.
operational_recommendation: Implement DSD streaming in the mini-app CLI compiler and container service-to-view message pipeline.
superapp_applicability: Container: manages high-speed byte streams between Service Worker logic and WebView renderer. Store: profiles package bundle sizes and streaming hydration compliance. Runtime: parses DSD chunks natively.

title: Super-app third-party widget isolation enforces closed shadow roots and CSS containment to prevent UI spoofing
summary: Container-enforced Shadow DOM encapsulation and CSS containment isolate third-party mini-app widgets from host UI chrome and sibling extensions.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Super-apps frequently host third-party embedded micro-widgets (e.g. mini-cards in feed, payment snippets, checkout buttons) that run in shared host pages: (1) Clickjacking & Style Spoofing Risks: Without DOM boundary enforcement, third-party CSS can inject rules modifying host checkout buttons, positioning transparent overlays, or sniffing host input focus; (2) Closed Shadow Root Boundaries: Container wraps untrusted embedded widgets inside closed Shadow DOM (`shadowrootmode="closed"`), hiding internal DOM nodes from sibling scripts and external `element.shadowRoot` inspection; (3) CSS Containment Directives: Host enforces `contain: content;` (combining layout, style, and paint containment) on all third-party widget containers, ensuring internal DOM changes cannot trigger full-page reflows; (4) Event Retargeting: Shadow DOM automatically retargets internal events (e.g. click coordinates, internal target IDs) to the host custom element, preventing third-party widgets from leaking internal structure. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Platform security controls: (1) Store automated package scanner validates that third-party card extensions comply with strict shadow root isolation; (2) Rejects packages attempting to register custom elements matching reserved super-app platform namespaces.
standard_reference: Super-App Embedded Widget Isolation & Component Security Architecture
relevance: Prevents UI redressing, CSS spoofing, and event sniffing across multi-tenant super-app feed widgets.
operational_recommendation: Require closed shadow roots and CSS layout containment on all embedded feed cards and third-party widgets.
superapp_applicability: Container: enforces closed shadow boundaries and event retargeting on embedded views. Store: blocks illegal custom element names and unencapsulated CSS rules. Runtime: guarantees isolated layout recalculation.

title: WHATWG Navigator.registerProtocolHandler standardizes web-based custom scheme registration and replacement tokens
summary: WHATWG HTML Living Standard specifies navigator.registerProtocolHandler(scheme, url) for registering web apps as URL scheme handlers with %s token interpolation.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The WHATWG HTML Living Standard (§8.8.1.3 Custom handlers / `registerProtocolHandler`) defines the client-side mechanism for registering applications as custom URL scheme handlers: (1) Method Signature: `navigator.registerProtocolHandler(scheme, url)` allows web applications to register themselves as handlers for specific URI schemes; (2) Scheme Whitelist & Prefix Rules: Supported schemes include either pre-approved standard schemes (e.g. 'mailto', 'irc', 'magnet', 'news', 'sip', 'sms', 'tel') or custom schemes prefixed strictly with `web+` or `ext+` followed by lowercase ASCII letters (e.g. 'web+pay', 'web+miniapp'); (3) Token Interpolation Syntax: The `url` argument must contain `%s` as an exact placeholder token; when the user triggers a link matching the registered scheme, the browser escapes the full target URI and substitutes it into `%s`; (4) Same-Origin Requirement: The destination `url` string must be strictly same-origin with the registering document, preventing third-party domain hijacking. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Native container bridge adaptation: (1) Native super-app container exposes a sandboxed protocol registration API mapping web+ schemes directly to OS intent filters and internal routing tables; (2) Enforces strict %s sanitization to prevent URL injection.
standard_reference: WHATWG HTML Living Standard §8.8.1.3 (Custom handlers)
relevance: Provides the web platform standard for seamless deep-link scheme delegation and web app intent handling.
operational_recommendation: Implement container-level registerProtocolHandler proxying with strict web+ prefix validation and %s URI escape verification.
superapp_applicability: Container: routes registered scheme intents into targeted mini-app WebViews. Store: records registered custom schemes during store manifest review. Runtime: manages active protocol mappings in container storage.

title: W3C Web App Manifest protocol_handlers member defines declarative install-time scheme binding
summary: W3C Web App Manifest standardizes the protocol_handlers dictionary member, enabling declarative protocol registration upon mini-app installation.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The W3C Web App Manifest specification standardizes the `protocol_handlers` member for declarative, install-time URL scheme associations: (1) Manifest Member Schema: Specified as an array of handler dictionaries: `"protocol_handlers": [ { "protocol": "web+tea", "url": "/tea?type=%s" } ]`; (2) Pre-Installation Verification: Unlike imperative JS calls that trigger disruptive browser permission popups, declarative manifest registration is evaluated and approved atomically during app installation or container provisioning; (3) URL Resolution & Scope: The `url` property is resolved against the manifest's `start_url` and must remain strictly within the manifest's defined `scope`; (4) Uninstallation Cleanup: Removing or updating the application automatically unbinds its registered protocol handlers from the operating system or host environment, eliminating orphaned link handlers. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Super-app catalog ingestion: (1) Store ingestion pipeline parses `protocol_handlers` during package submission, registering the mini-app in the super-app global intent router; (2) Automatically rejects submissions that attempt to claim reserved protocol names without enterprise partner privileges.
standard_reference: W3C Web App Manifest Specification (§protocol_handlers member)
relevance: Enables zero-friction deep-link handling without requiring imperative JavaScript registration routines upon every launch.
operational_recommendation: Standardize protocol_handlers array in mini-app manifest.json as the canonical mechanism for custom scheme routing.
superapp_applicability: Container: reads protocol_handlers from app.json/manifest.json at package install. Store: validates scheme uniqueness and resolves domain collisions. Runtime: maps incoming deep links directly to target routes.

title: Protocol handler dispatch security enforces scheme ownership verification, open-redirect defense, and URI decoding sanitization
summary: Super-app deep link router implements strict scheme ownership verification, input parameter sanitization, and open redirect defenses.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Invoking custom protocol handlers introduces critical attack vectors, including scheme hijacking, parameter injection, cross-site scripting (XSS), and SSRF: (1) Scheme Squatting Mitigation: Malicious mini-apps may register schemes like `web+bank` to intercept sensitive financial transactions; the store maintains an authoritative, cryptographically signed scheme registry where verified corporate publishers have exclusive ownership of declared schemes; (2) Input Sanitization & Decoding: The container decodes the `%s` payload using strict URI parsing algorithms, rejecting control characters, CRLF injection, javascript: pseudo-schemes, and malformed UTF-8 sequences; (3) Open Redirect Prevention: Handler target URLs cannot accept external unvalidated redirection parameters; all intermediate navigation hops must remain within the mini-app's verified domain scope; (4) User Consent Dialogs: For sensitive or cross-publisher scheme invocations, the container displays a confirmation bottom-sheet stating the calling application ID and destination mini-app title. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Container gateway security: (1) All custom protocol dispatches pass through a central native routing filter; (2) Intercepts and logs any anomalous burst invocations.
standard_reference: OWASP Mobile Application Security Verification Standard (MASVS-PLATFORM) & Protocol Handler Security Guidelines
relevance: Prevents unauthorized intent interception, parameter tampering, and phishing across inter-app deep links.
operational_recommendation: Enforce verified publisher ownership for all custom schemes in the mini-app store and sanitize %s arguments at the native router layer.
superapp_applicability: Container: filters and sanitizes incoming scheme parameters before dispatching to WebViews. Store: manages exclusive scheme reservation and namespace disputes. Runtime: prompts user for cross-publisher launches.

title: Inter-mini-app protocol invocation contracts establish cryptographically attested caller handles and structured response callbacks
summary: Container-mediated inter-mini-app scheme invocations pass signed caller attestation tokens and structured callback handles for two-way workflow completion.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Complex super-app ecosystems require seamless interoperability between decoupled mini-apps (e.g. Ride-Hailing app invoking Navigation Mini-App, E-Commerce invoking FinTech Payment Mini-App): (1) Calling Scheme Invocation: Caller invokes `superapp.navigateToMiniApp({ protocol: 'web+pay://checkout?orderId=123', callbackUrl: '/payment-result' })`; (2) Cryptographic Caller Attestation: Container native router injects a signed caller token (JWT signed with container private key) into the destination mini-app's launch arguments, proving the exact `callerAppId`, tenant domain, and user authorization scope; (3) Opaque Result Handlers: Destination mini-app executes the transaction and invokes `superapp.returnResult({ transactionId: 'TX789', status: 'SUCCESS' })`; (4) Automatic Back-Stack Restoration: Container closes the destination view and delivers the structured response payload back to the calling mini-app's resumed context without reloading page state. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Platform SDK contracts: (1) Standardizes inter-app protocol schemas across the super-app ecosystem; (2) Restricts cross-app invoking permissions via manifest capability grants.
standard_reference: Super-App Inter-Application Invocation & Attested Workflow Standard
relevance: Enables modular micro-frontend super-app architectures while guaranteeing authenticated, tamper-proof inter-app transactions.
operational_recommendation: Deploy container-level caller attestation tokens and opaque result callback channels for all inter-mini-app deep links.
superapp_applicability: Container: mints caller attestation tokens and manages UI stack navigation between mini-apps. Store: validates inter-app permission grants. Runtime: exposes typed invocation and returnResult APIs.

title: Super-app protocol registry architecture coordinates intent disambiguation, default handler preferences, and remote revocation
summary: Super-app protocol registry manages intent filters, user disambiguation prompts when multiple handlers register the same scheme, and emergency remote revocation.
detail: [SPEC FACT] When multiple mini-apps register handling capabilities for shared standard or generic protocols (e.g. `web+map` registered by both Google Maps Mini-App and Grab Maps Mini-App): (1) Intent Filter Matching Engine: Container maintains an in-memory intent routing table evaluating scheme, authority, path pattern, and MIME type filters; (2) User Disambiguation Dialog: If multiple handlers qualify, container presents a native 'Open with...' bottom-sheet allowing the user to select their preferred mini-app ('Just Once' or 'Always'); (3) User Preference Persistence: Persistent choices are recorded in container storage and exposed in super-app user settings for subsequent re-configuration; (4) Emergency Remote Revocation: If an approved mini-app is compromised or hijacked, super-app operators can push a signed protocol revocation notice from the store console, instantly stripping the app's scheme associations across all installed clients without requiring a full app store binary release. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Store governance tools: (1) Operator console monitors protocol conflict metrics; (2) Enforces trademark protection and fair competition policies across protocol handler declarations.
standard_reference: Super-App Intent Routing Architecture & Protocol Disambiguation Framework
relevance: Provides robust, conflict-free multi-handler resolution and real-time operational safety for super-app ecosystems.
operational_recommendation: Implement container-level intent disambiguation dialogs with user default preferences and store-driven remote scheme revocation.

title: WICG launch_handler manifest member standardizes client routing modes for existing and new container contexts
summary: WICG Web App Launch specification defines launch_handler client_mode policies governing how container runtimes route incoming launches.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The WICG Web App Launch specification introduces the `launch_handler` member in the Web App Manifest, allowing web mini-apps to control how external launch triggers (deep links, app shortcuts, share targets) are dispatched. The key property `client_mode` accepts single values or fallback sequences: (1) `auto`: Browser/container determines routing behaviour based on platform conventions; (2) `navigate-new`: Creates a new top-level browsing context (new WebView tab/page) loaded with the launch target URL; (3) `navigate-existing`: Focuses the most recently interacted existing browsing context of the application and immediately navigates it to the launch target URL, discarding ongoing transient state; (4) `focus-existing`: Focuses an existing browsing context without reloading or navigating away from the current document, instead enqueuing a launch event to be consumed by script via the LaunchQueue API. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Super-app container routing engine: (1) Reads manifest `launch_handler.client_mode` during mini-app package compilation; (2) Enforces `focus-existing` as the default for productivity and multi-step transactional mini-apps (e.g. food delivery, banking) to preserve form state and checkout progress.
standard_reference: WICG Web App Launch Specification & W3C Web App Manifest
relevance: Provides standardized, declarative window routing policies preventing duplicate instance thrashing and unwanted page reloads.
operational_recommendation: Configure container window manager to honor launch_handler.client_mode declarations and default to focus-existing for in-flight sessions.
superapp_applicability: Container: routes deep links and push intents to active WebViews based on client_mode. Store: validates launch_handler manifest syntax during submission. Runtime: implements window focus and context restoration.

title: LaunchQueue API provides deterministic parameter queuing and consumer registration without startup race conditions
summary: window.launchQueue buffers incoming LaunchParams until the mini-app registers a consumer callback, eliminating hydration timing vulnerabilities.
detail: [SPEC FACT] To decouple application boot sequence and framework hydration from asynchronous incoming launch events, the WICG specification defines the `LaunchQueue` interface exposed at `window.launchQueue`. Features include: (1) Parameter Queuing: When an app is launched with target URLs or file handles, the runtime generates a `LaunchParams` object and appends it to an internal FIFO launch queue; (2) Consumer Registration: Mini-app script calls `window.launchQueue.setConsumer((launchParams) => { ... })` once initialization, authentication checks, and DOM hydration are complete; (3) Replay Guarantee: If launch events arrive before `setConsumer()` is invoked (e.g., during cold start), they are buffered indefinitely until a consumer is set, at which point the queued params are replayed synchronously in arrival order; (4) Consumer Immutability: Calling `setConsumer()` replaces any previously registered callback, ensuring a single authoritative routing handler handles subsequent warm launches throughout the document lifecycle. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Container bootstrap runtime: (1) Synthesizes `window.launchQueue` polyfill/shim on top of native bridge for legacy WebView engines; (2) Enforces a 5-second queue drain watchdog, emitting telemetry if mini-app scripts fail to register a consumer.
standard_reference: WICG Web App Launch — LaunchQueue Interface
relevance: Eliminates race conditions where deep-link arguments and file payloads are dropped during complex framework hydration.
operational_recommendation: Mandate launchQueue consumer registration in mini-app SDK bootstrap templates to guarantee reliable deep-link handling.
superapp_applicability: Container: holds native launch parameters in memory until WebView bridge signals consumer readiness. Store: checks SDK version compatibility. Runtime: exposes typed window.launchQueue.

title: LaunchParams interface conveys structured target URLs and read-only file system handles to running instances
summary: LaunchParams objects provide targetURL strings and FileSystemHandle sequences directly to the consumer callback for safe processing.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The `LaunchParams` object passed to the `LaunchQueue` consumer contains structured metadata describing the invocation trigger: (1) `targetURL`: A read-only DOMString representing the full resolved URL that triggered the launch, including query parameters, fragments, and routing path (e.g. `https://shop.superapp.vn/items/456?promo=SUMMER`); (2) `files`: A frozen array of `FileSystemHandle` (or `FileSystemFileHandle`) objects representing files passed via OS file associations, Web Share Target, or host container file pickers; (3) Sandboxed File Permissions: File handles delivered via `LaunchParams` grant scoped read access (and optional write access subject to user confirmation) without exposing native platform filesystem directory trees; (4) URL Parsing Hygiene: Mini-apps parse `launchParams.targetURL` using the standard `new URL(launchParams.targetURL)` constructor, allowing internal routers (React Router, Vue Router) to transition views dynamically without triggering full HTTP round-trips. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Native container URL dispatch: (1) Sanitizes incoming URLs against scheme allowlists before wrapping into LaunchParams; (2) Attaches signed tenant authentication tokens to `targetURL` query parameters when cross-app SSO is requested.
standard_reference: WICG Web App Launch — LaunchParams Interface & File Handling Integration
relevance: Standardizes payload delivery for deep links and shared files into running mini-app instances without context teardown.
operational_recommendation: Use LaunchParams.targetURL for client-side routing transitions in single-instance mini-apps.
superapp_applicability: Container: extracts query parameters and file descriptors and serializes them into LaunchParams. Store: audits file handler manifest declarations. Runtime: binds parameters to client router.

title: Container task stack architectures balance single-instance resource efficiency against multi-window concurrency
summary: Super-app container managers enforce single-instance or multi-instance window routing to manage device RAM, task stacks, and user workflows.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Super-apps manage dozens of embedded mini-apps within a single native operating system process or process tree, necessitating explicit container instance routing strategies: (1) Single-Instance Model (`focus-existing` / Android `singleTask` equivalent): Only one active WebView instance of a given `miniAppId` is permitted in memory; incoming deep links bring the existing instance to the top of the container stack and dispatch a warm launch event; this conserves mobile RAM, prevents fragmented local storage states, and preserves active checkout or audio playback; (2) Multi-Instance Model (`navigate-new` / Android `standard` equivalent): Each launch opens an independent container tab/view with its own isolated memory heap; suitable for comparing products, viewing multiple documents, or running concurrent isolated utilities; (3) Memory Threshold Clamping: Container managers enforce a global cap on open instances (e.g. maximum 5 concurrent mini-app WebViews); when a new instance is launched exceeding the threshold, the container evicts the least-recently-used (LRU) single-instance background context using graceful lifecycle teardown. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Host navigation orchestrator: (1) Maps manifest `launch_handler` settings to native Activity/ViewController task affinity; (2) Maintains a back-stack registry routing system back gestures seamlessly across multi-instance hierarchies.
standard_reference: Super-App Container Window Routing Architecture & WICG Launch Handler Guidelines
relevance: Prevents catastrophic memory bloat and navigation state corruption caused by unrestricted multi-window spawning.
operational_recommendation: Enforce single-instance routing by default with LRU background eviction and warm launch parameter dispatching.
superapp_applicability: Container: maintains instance registry, enforces window limits, and reuses warm WebViews. Store: provides developer toggles for multi-window entitlement. Runtime: notifies app of stack focus changes.

title: Cross-ecosystem launch lifecycle convergence aligns WICG Web App Launch with WeChat onShow and Alipay app routing
summary: Harmonizing WICG LaunchQueue with WeChat App.onShow and Alipay my.onAppShow establishes cross-platform mini-app launch parity.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Major production super-apps have proprietary lifecycle hooks that map directly to the WICG Web App Launch standard: (1) WeChat Mini-Program Lifecycle: Cold launch triggers `App.onLaunch(options)` followed by `App.onShow(options)`; warm re-launches (e.g. user taps another deep link, scans a QR code, or returns from an external share) bypass `onLaunch` and invoke `App.onShow(options)` with updated `options.query`, `options.scene`, and `options.referrerInfo`; (2) Alipay Mini-Program Lifecycle: Employs `my.onAppShow((options) => ...)` and `my.ix.onAppRoute` providing launch arguments and entry paths; (3) Architectural Convergence: The WICG `launch_handler: { client_mode: 'focus-existing' }` plus `window.launchQueue.setConsumer(params)` serves as the open web standard equivalent of `App.onShow(options)`; (4) Unified SDK Abstraction: A standard super-app container provides an abstraction bridge where a single unified launch event listener (`superapp.onLaunch((params) => ...)` or standard `launchQueue.setConsumer`) works identically across proprietary mini-program runtimes and standard Chromium/WebKit WebViews, passing entry scene IDs, referral caller attestation, and query parameters. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Developer platform compatibility layer: (1) Transpiles proprietary `onShow` calls to `launchQueue` semantics; (2) Injects standard scene tracking headers into analytics pipelines.
standard_reference: Super-App Universal Mini-App Lifecycle Standard & WICG Launch Handler Alignment
relevance: Enables seamless portability of mini-app codebases across WeChat, Alipay, and open web super-app containers.
operational_recommendation: Adopt WICG launchQueue semantics as the underlying runtime standard while providing backward-compatible onShow bridge adapters.
superapp_applicability: Container: translates native intent extras into standard LaunchParams and onShow option dictionaries. Store: validates lifecycle declarations. Runtime: dispatches unified launch events.

title: WICG Page Lifecycle specification formalizes six discrete states and lifecycle transition events for containerized contexts
summary: WICG Page Lifecycle defines Active, Passive, Hidden, Frozen, Terminated, and Discarded states governing CPU, timer, and memory allowances.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The WICG Page Lifecycle specification models the complete execution continuum of a web application to enable proactive OS resource management: (1) `Active`: Document is visible in the foreground and has user input focus; all JavaScript, WebGL, media, and animation timers run unrestricted; (2) `Passive`: Document is visible but does not have input focus (e.g. modal overlay, picture-in-picture, split-screen UI); UI rendering occurs, but high-impact background compute is de-prioritized; (3) `Hidden`: Document is not visible to the user (e.g. covered by another mini-app, super-app minimized to background, screen locked); dispatched via `visibilitychange` (`document.visibilityState === 'hidden'`); (4) `Frozen`: Execution is suspended by the browser engine; CPU timers (`setTimeout`, `setInterval`), promises, and network callbacks are halted, but DOM tree and JS heap remain intact in RAM; (5) `Terminated`: Document is unloaded and torn down from memory via `pagehide`; (6) `Discarded`: The browser/container unloads the page and reclaims memory due to OS memory pressure, retaining tab identity and entry state for subsequent restoration. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Super-app container lifecycle monitor: (1) Orchestrates state transitions in synchronization with native mobile lifecycle; (2) Emits `freeze` and `resume` events into WebView JavaScript runtimes.
standard_reference: WICG Page Lifecycle Specification & W3C Page Visibility API
relevance: Provides a mathematically defined state machine eliminating undefined behavior during mobile backgrounding and low-memory conditions.
operational_recommendation: Implement formal Active-Passive-Hidden-Frozen-Terminated state machine transitions across all container WebView hosts.
superapp_applicability: Container: drives WebView state transitions based on OS window focus and backgrounding events. Store: audits lifecycle event compliance. Runtime: exposes freeze and resume document listeners.

title: Native memory pressure integration translates Android onTrimMemory and iOS memory warnings into progressive WebView eviction
summary: Super-app containers bridge Android ComponentCallbacks2 and iOS memory warnings into tiered cache clearing, freezing, and background discarding.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Mobile operating systems notify parent applications when RAM thresholds are crossed, requiring super-app containers to actively govern nested mini-app processes: (1) Android `ComponentCallbacks2.onTrimMemory(level)`: Level `TRIM_MEMORY_RUNNING_MODERATE` triggers container internal image/bitmap cache flushes; `TRIM_MEMORY_RUNNING_LOW` and `TRIM_MEMORY_RUNNING_CRITICAL` trigger aggressive DOM cache trimming and transition offscreen WebViews from `Hidden` to `Frozen`; (2) Android Background Trimming: `TRIM_MEMORY_BACKGROUND` and `TRIM_MEMORY_MODERATE` trigger saving state snapshots and unloading offscreen mini-apps with `TRIM_MEMORY_COMPLETE` prompting immediate termination of all non-essential background WebViews; (3) iOS Memory Handling: `UIApplicationDelegate.applicationDidReceiveMemoryWarning(_:)` and `didReceiveMemoryWarning()` in `UIViewController` trigger container-level purging of WebKit cache, decoded image memory, and unloading hidden `WKWebView` instances; (4) Container Bridge Protocol: The native container sends a high-priority synthetic message `superapp.onMemoryPressure({ level: 'critical' })` across the JS bridge, allowing mini-apps to serialize transient data and release large WebGL buffers before native process termination. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Memory governor daemon: (1) Monitored via native memory profiling; (2) Automatically terminates runaway mini-apps exceeding 150MB RSS.
standard_reference: Android ComponentCallbacks2 Architecture & Apple UIKit Memory Management Standard
relevance: Prevents catastrophic host process termination (Out-Of-Memory / OOM crashes) caused by unmanaged multi-mini-app memory footprints.
operational_recommendation: Bind native onTrimMemory and memory warning hooks directly to container WebView freezing and background discarding pipelines.
superapp_applicability: Container: listens to OS memory pressure signals, flushes native caches, and signals WebViews. Store: enforces memory quota limits. Runtime: provides memory warning event hooks to mini-app code.

title: Deterministic background freezing suspends timers, WebGL contexts, and media pipelines while preserving state in RAM
summary: Freezing transitions halt CPU execution, throttle background battery drain, and guarantee clean state preservation before suspension.
detail: [SPEC FACT] When a mini-app transitions from `Hidden` to `Frozen`, the browser/container enforces deterministic execution boundaries to prevent background CPU drain and battery depletion: (1) JavaScript Suspension: All active timers (`setTimeout`, `setInterval`), animation frames (`requestAnimationFrame`), and queued macro-tasks are frozen at their current state and resumed without catch-up storming upon waking; (2) WebGL & Canvas Context Preservation: WebGL textures and canvas state are kept resident in GPU/system RAM, avoiding expensive shader re-compilation, but rendering loops are paused; (3) Media & Audio Teardown: Audio contexts not associated with declared background audio permissions are paused immediately; (4) The `freeze` and `resume` Lifecycle Events: Before pausing execution, the document fires the `freeze` event (`document.addEventListener('freeze', (event) => { ... })`), allowing the application to close IndexedDB connections, persist dirty state, and flush pending telemetry. When brought back to foreground, the document fires the `resume` event (`document.addEventListener('resume', (event) => { ... })`). [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Container background execution watchdog: (1) Enforces a strict 3-second timeout on the `freeze` event handler, force-pausing the WebView if JavaScript fails to yield; (2) Enforces zero background CPU utilization for unprivileged mini-apps.
standard_reference: WICG Page Lifecycle Specification — Freeze and Resume Event Contracts
relevance: Guarantees zero battery drain and CPU consumption for background mini-apps while maintaining instant foreground resumption.
operational_recommendation: Utilize freeze/resume event lifecycles with hard 3-second grace periods to safely pause background mini-app operations.
superapp_applicability: Container: pauses and resumes WebView execution threads and WebGL contexts. Store: tests background battery impact during review. Runtime: fires freeze/resume events to script.

title: State restoration contracts utilize document.wasDiscarded and persistent session storage to transparently recover evicted instances
summary: document.wasDiscarded allows mini-apps to detect low-memory process teardown and seamlessly restore UI state from local persistence.
detail: [SPEC FACT] When native memory pressure forces the container to transition a frozen mini-app into the `Discarded` state, the entire browsing context and JavaScript heap are destroyed. To provide a seamless user experience when the user returns to the tab: (1) The `document.wasDiscarded` Property: The WICG Page Lifecycle specification introduces the boolean `document.wasDiscarded` on the Document interface, which evaluates to `true` if the current navigation is restoring a document that was previously discarded by the user agent due to resource constraints; (2) Persistent State Hydration: During startup, if `document.wasDiscarded === true`, mini-app initialization logic reads saved form fields, scroll positions, navigation depth, and user inputs from `sessionStorage` or `IndexedDB`, restoring the UI to the exact pre-discard state; (3) State Serialization Hooks: Applications use the `pagehide` (with `event.persisted === true` check) or `freeze` events to synchronously commit serialized state snapshots into persistent storage before discarding occurs; (4) Telemetry & Diagnostics: Super-app platforms monitor discard-to-launch ratios (`wasDiscarded` frequency) across device RAM tiers (e.g. 2GB vs 8GB phones) to calibrate container background eviction policies. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Platform persistence engine: (1) Allocates a dedicated 2MB `sessionStorage` slot per mini-app guaranteed against clearing during background discards; (2) Provides automated scroll-position restoration.
standard_reference: WICG Page Lifecycle Specification — Discarded State and Restoration Protocol
relevance: Eliminates jarring app restarts and lost form data when background mini-apps are killed under mobile memory pressure.
operational_recommendation: Integrate document.wasDiscarded checks into mini-app boot sequence and automate session state restoration.
superapp_applicability: Container: sets wasDiscarded flag when reloading previously killed background tabs. Store: validates presence of state restoration logic. Runtime: exposes wasDiscarded property.

title: Super-app background policy framework governs maximum residence timers, graceful termination, and privileged background tasks
summary: Super-app governance enforces a 5-minute background residence limit, graceful termination protocols, and strict exemptions for background audio/location.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Super-apps balance device stability and background functionality through formal background residence policies (modeled on WeChat and Alipay industry standards): (1) Maximum Residence Timer: Unprivileged mini-apps transitioned to the background have a default 5-minute grace period in the `Frozen` state; if the user does not return within 300 seconds, the container initiates a graceful `Terminated` teardown, freeing WebView resources; (2) Privileged Background Exceptions: Mini-apps declaring specific background capabilities (e.g., continuous background music via `wx.getBackgroundAudioManager()`, navigation turn-by-turn audio, or active VOIP calls) receive persistent execution leases, bypassing automatic 5-minute teardown; (3) Clean Resource Deallocation: Upon termination, the container destroys the WebView instance, detaches all JS bridge event listeners, releases hardware camera/microphone locks, and tears down WebSocket connections; (4) Crash Loop Protection: If a mini-app crashes repeatedly during background-to-foreground transitions (>2 crashes within 60 seconds), the container quarantines the app, clears its corrupted transient cache, and forces a clean cold restart. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Operator governance policy: (1) Background audio and location permissions undergo manual review before store approval; (2) Real-time background CPU monitoring terminates violating instances.
standard_reference: Super-App Background Execution Policy & Resource Governance Standard
relevance: Maintains super-app operating stability, battery efficiency, and device responsiveness during long-running background sessions.
operational_recommendation: Enforce a 5-minute frozen background residence ceiling with auditable permission exemptions for audio and navigation.
superapp_applicability: Container: manages background timers and terminates expired WebViews. Store: reviews background capability declarations. Runtime: provides background execution status signals.

title: WICG Digital Goods API defines payment-provider service binding for web and mini-app in-app purchase ecosystems
summary: window.getDigitalGoodsService binds web mini-apps to host payment services, establishing a secure bridge for digital merchandising.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The WICG Digital Goods API specification provides an ergonomic JavaScript interface allowing web applications and mini-apps to interact with digital storefront billing engines (e.g. Google Play Billing, Apple StoreKit, or native Super-App Wallet): (1) Service Discovery: The application queries `window.getDigitalGoodsService(paymentMethod)`, where `paymentMethod` is a standard payment method identifier URL (such as `"https://play.google.com/billing"` or `"https://superapp.com/billing"`); (2) Capability Verification: If the host platform supports digital goods for that provider, the promise resolves to a `DigitalGoodsService` instance; if unsupported or disabled, it returns `null`, enabling graceful fallback to web-based checkout flows; (3) Sandboxed Origin Isolation: Service binding verifies that the calling origin matches the registered mini-app publisher credentials, preventing unauthorized third-party iframes from initiating SKU queries or purchases; (4) Container Bridge Adaptation: In super-app containers, the host injects a native `DigitalGoodsService` proxy conforming directly to the WICG interface, bridging mini-app JavaScript calls directly to the host operating system's in-app billing subsystem. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Container billing gateway: (1) Inspects mini-app digital goods declarations in the store manifest; (2) Enforces store-level merchant account associations.
standard_reference: WICG Digital Goods API Specification & W3C Payment Request Architecture
relevance: Standardizes in-app digital product discovery and transaction initiation across multi-platform web containers.
operational_recommendation: Implement window.getDigitalGoodsService in the mini-app JSAPI to bind web apps to the host super-app billing provider.
superapp_applicability: Container: intercepts getDigitalGoodsService and binds to native billing libraries. Store: manages SKU catalogs and revenue shares. Runtime: exposes standard promise-based API.

title: DigitalGoodsService.getDetails returns standardized SKU metadata, introductory pricing, and localized subscription periods
summary: getDetails retrieves ItemDetails dictionaries containing localized currency, pricing, and billing periods directly from the host store.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The `DigitalGoodsService.getDetails(itemIds)` method takes an array of SKU strings and returns a promise resolving to an array of `ItemDetails` objects: (1) `itemId`: The unique string identifier of the SKU declared in the mini-app store catalog; (2) `title` and `description`: Store-provided localized product naming and marketing copy; (3) `price`: A `PaymentCurrencyAmount` object containing the `currency` code (ISO 4217, e.g. 'VND', 'USD') and numeric `value` formatted as a string; (4) Subscription Metadata: For recurring digital goods, `ItemDetails` provides `subscriptionPeriod` (ISO 8601 duration format, e.g. 'P1M' for one month, 'P1Y' for one year), `freeTrialPeriod`, and `introductoryPrice` (including period and cycle count); (5) Zero Backend Overhead: Mini-app frontends display exact user-localized currencies, tax inclusions, and regional pricing tiers without requiring custom server-side geo-pricing lookups. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Store catalog management: (1) Centralizes SKU registration in the super-app publisher console; (2) Synchronizes pricing tiers across regional exchange rates and local value-added taxes (VAT).
standard_reference: WICG Digital Goods API — ItemDetails and Pricing Models
relevance: Eliminates hardcoded currency formatting and provides compliant, localized price presentations across international markets.
operational_recommendation: Query getDetails dynamically before rendering store UI to ensure price and subscription terms match user billing region.
superapp_applicability: Container: fetches SKU metadata from host billing cache. Store: provides developer catalog management and regional price matrices. Runtime: returns typed ItemDetails.

title: W3C Payment Request pairing completes in-app purchases and issues cryptographically signed purchase tokens
summary: Purchases are initiated via PaymentRequest with provider methodData, returning signed purchase tokens for backend verification.
detail: [SPEC FACT] In accordance with WICG and W3C standards, purchasing a digital good is executed via the `PaymentRequest` API rather than a bespoke method on `DigitalGoodsService`: (1) Invocation: The mini-app constructs a `PaymentRequest` with `methodData: [{ supportedMethods: 'https://superapp.com/billing', data: { sku: 'gem_pack_100', developerPayload: 'order_uuid_xyz' } }]`; (2) User Interaction: Calling `paymentRequest.show()` opens the native host payment sheet (displaying user biometrics, saved card, or super-app wallet balance); (3) Response Payload: Upon successful authorization, the promise resolves to a `PaymentResponse` whose `details` payload contains `purchaseToken`, `orderId`, and `signature`; (4) Cryptographic Verification: Mini-app client code transmits `purchaseToken` to its secure backend server; the backend verifies the token directly against the super-app billing server via mutual TLS / OAuth 2.0 Open API; (5) Transaction Completion: The client invokes `paymentResponse.complete('success')` to dismiss the payment UI. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Container security architecture: (1) Locks payment sheet invocation behind user gesture activation (`isTrusted: true`); (2) Mitigates clickjacking via native overlay protections.
standard_reference: W3C Payment Request API & WICG Digital Goods Integration
relevance: Unifies web payment semantics with native mobile billing engines, guaranteeing cryptographic tamper-resistance.
operational_recommendation: Execute all digital good purchases through W3C PaymentRequest with mandatory server-side purchase token validation.
superapp_applicability: Container: hosts native payment sheet and mediates biometric authentication. Store: verifies transaction signatures. Runtime: handles PaymentResponse lifecycle.

title: Entitlement lifecycle protocols govern consumable delivery, non-consumable acknowledgement, and refund mitigation
summary: DigitalGoodsService consume and acknowledge APIs manage entitlement lifecycle, preventing duplicate grants and automated refund chargebacks.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The Digital Goods API defines explicit methods to manage the post-purchase entitlement lifecycle: (1) `listPurchases()`: Returns an array of current, active `PurchaseDetails` (items owned by the user that have not been consumed, or active subscriptions); vital for restoring purchases across device switches; (2) `listPurchaseHistory()`: Returns the historical record of all past purchases, including consumed items; (3) `consume(purchaseToken)`: Consumes a consumable product (e.g. in-game currency, temporary boosts), marking the token as consumed on the billing server so the item can be purchased again by the user; (4) Mandatory Acknowledgement (`acknowledge` / server-side acknowledge): Modeled after Google Play Billing rules, non-consumable items and subscriptions MUST be explicitly acknowledged within a 3-day statutory window; failure to acknowledge results in automatic transaction cancellation and fund refunds to the user; (5) Server-Side vs Client-Side Reconciliation: While `DigitalGoodsService` provides client methods, enterprise super-app governance mandates that critical entitlement grants and consumptions occur via server-to-server webhook APIs to prevent client-side bypass. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Billing engine reconciliation: (1) Monitors unacknowledged transaction queues; (2) Sends push notifications and automated alerts for pending consumable grants.
standard_reference: WICG Digital Goods API — Purchase Management & Google Play Billing Lifecycle
relevance: Prevents catastrophic revenue leakage, ungranted purchase disputes, and double-spending of consumable digital goods.
operational_recommendation: Implement strict acknowledge and consume protocols backed by server-to-server webhook verification.
superapp_applicability: Container: proxies consume and listPurchases calls to host store billing engine. Store: tracks acknowledgment timeouts and processes refunds. Runtime: returns typed PurchaseDetails.

title: Multi-tenant settlement governance establishes split ledgering, platform commissions, escrow reserves, and dispute arbitration
summary: Super-app settlement systems enforce real-time split ledgering, platform fee deductions (e.g. 15-30%), rolling escrow reserves, and tax compliance.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Commercial operation of a multi-tenant mini-app store requires robust financial settlement and ledgering governance (modeled on WeChat Mini-Programs, Apple StoreKit, and Google Play Store policies): (1) Split Ledgering: For every completed digital good purchase, the super-app billing engine automatically splits the gross transaction amount: deducting platform commission (e.g. 15% for micro-merchants / 30% standard), payment gateway fees (1-2%), and applicable withholding/VAT taxes, routing the net balance to the developer's ledger; (2) Rolling Escrow & Chargeback Reserves: A configurable rolling reserve (e.g. 5-10% of gross volume held for 30-60 days) is maintained to absorb customer chargebacks, friendly fraud, and disputed refund requests; (3) Payout Evidence & Invoicing: Monthly automated settlement statements generate cryptographic audit trails, supporting automated e-invoicing compliant with national tax authorities (e.g. Vietnam General Department of Taxation Decree 123/2020/ND-CP); (4) Developer Dispute Arbitration: Transparent merchant consoles provide dispute ticketing, chargeback evidence submission workflows, and anti-fraud velocity limits mitigating stolen credit card testing. [SUPER-APP CONTROL] Operator financial ledger: (1) Implements double-entry bookkeeping; (2) Isolates client funds in segregated fiduciary accounts.
standard_reference: Super-App Financial Settlement & Multi-Tenant Storefront Ledgering Standard
relevance: Provides the essential financial infrastructure and regulatory tax compliance necessary for operating a commercial mini-app store.
operational_recommendation: Deploy double-entry split ledgering with automated tax deduction, rolling chargeback reserves, and developer dispute consoles.
superapp_applicability: Container: presents localized total prices including applicable VAT. Store: runs automated settlement batches, commission withholding, and payout reporting. Runtime: transmits order UUID.

title: WICG Attribution Reporting API Architecture: Source Registration, Trigger Registration, and Event-Level vs Aggregatable Conversion Delivery
summary: The WICG Attribution Reporting API enables privacy-preserving measurement of user conversions across web and mini-app contexts without third-party cookies or persistent cross-origin identifiers. Navigation and event sources are registered via 'Attribution-Reporting-Register-Source' response headers, while downstream conversion triggers are recorded via 'Attribution-Reporting-Register-Trigger' headers, allowing the client runtime to correlate source clicks/views with conversion events locally.
standards: RFC 8941 Structured Field Values for HTTP
key_points: Source registration occurs on navigation clicks or fetch requests emitting the Attribution-Reporting-Eligible request header and receiving Attribution-Reporting-Register-Source response headers containing source_event_id, destination, expiry, and priority.

Trigger registration occurs on conversion landing pages or transaction endpoints returning Attribution-Reporting-Register-Trigger headers with event_trigger_data, aggregatable_trigger_data, and debug_reporting flags.

Local client correlation eliminates third-party tracking: the user agent matches source and trigger origins based on top-level site matching rules, preventing ad networks from building cross-site behavioral dossiers.

title: Differential Privacy & Randomized Response: Event-Level Noise, Coarse Value Bucketing, and Delay-Randomized Postback Scheduling
summary: To prevent re-identification through high-entropy conversion feedback, the Attribution Reporting specification applies ε-differential privacy mechanisms. Event-level reports are bounded to 3 bits (8 conversion states) for click sources and 1 bit (2 conversion states) for view sources, with randomized response noise injected when report thresholds are breached. Delivery is scheduled across randomized multi-day windows to prevent traffic timing correlation.
key_points: Randomized response injects cryptographic noise where the client reports a completely random conversion state with probability p, providing ε-differential privacy guarantees against conversion tracking attacks.
Information entropy is strictly clamped: click-through attributions allow a maximum of 3 bits of conversion data (values 0-7), while view-through attributions allow only 1 bit (0 or 1).
Postback scheduling introduces deterministic delays partitioned into reporting windows (e.g. 2 days, 7 days, 30 days) combined with randomized jitter to defeat network packet correlation.

title: Aggregatable Reports & TEE Aggregation Service: 128-Bit Histogram Buckets, HPKE Payload Encryption, and Centralized Differential Privacy
summary: For rich, multi-dimensional conversion analytics (e.g., cart value, SKU categories, geographic region), the specification introduces Aggregatable Reports. Clients generate 128-bit histogram bucket contributions and encrypt the payload using Hybrid Public Key Encryption (HPKE). Decryption and aggregation can only occur inside a Trusted Execution Environment (TEE) run by an attested Aggregation Service, which adds Laplace noise and enforces strict query budgets.
standards: RFC 9458 Encrypted Client Hello / Privacy Pass
key_points: Aggregatable reports represent conversions as key-value pairs where the key is a 128-bit histogram bucket ID and the value is a bounded integer contribution (e.g., purchase value scaled to L1 budget).
Payloads are encrypted on-device using HPKE with public keys published by attested key management services, rendering the report unreadable to the publisher, super-app host, and ad-tech collector.

The Aggregation Service operates in a hardware TEE (AWS Nitro Enclaves or GCP Confidential Space), decrypting batched reports, computing aggregate sums, adding differential privacy noise, and enforcing single-use replay prevention.

title: Native Host Attribution Parity: Apple SKAdNetwork 4.0 / AdAttributionKit and Google Play Install Referrer API Integration
summary: Super-app mini-app containers must interoperate with native mobile OS attribution frameworks without violating App Store or Google Play tracking policies. Apple SKAdNetwork 4.0 / AdAttributionKit provides coarse conversion values (low/medium/high) and hierarchical source IDs, while Google Play Install Referrer API provides secure UTM parameter passing for mini-app campaigns launched from external channels.
standards: Google Play Install Referrer API v2.2
key_points: Apple SKAdNetwork 4.0 / AdAttributionKit utilizes hierarchical source identifiers (2 to 4 digits) and coarse conversion values (fine, low, medium, high) delivered across 3 distinct postback windows (0-2 days, 3-7 days, 8-35 days).

Google Play Install Referrer API provides cryptographically signed install referrer strings, click timestamps, and install begin timestamps, allowing the super-app host to attribute native app installs and mini-app activations.
Super-app host container policy must strictly forbid exchanging raw IDFA/AAID identifiers with mini-app third parties, mediating all external attribution through privacy-preserving OS APIs.

title: Super-App Attribution Gateway Architecture: Cryptographic Click Attestation, Host-Mediated Redirects, and Ad Fraud Mitigations
summary: To prevent click spoofing, impression laundering, and attribution fraud in the mini-app marketplace, the super-app host must deploy an Attribution Gateway. The gateway signs campaign navigation clicks with host asymmetric keys, enforces domain allowlisting for conversion landing pages, and filters bot traffic before attributing revenue shares or campaign incentives to publishers.
key_points: Host-mediated click signing injects cryptographic nonces and short-lived HMAC signatures into mini-app launch deep links, verifying that launches originated from legitimate user taps rather than background automated intents.
Mini-app conversion triggers are validated against registered manifest scopes and e-commerce checkout receipts, eliminating fictitious conversion claims by fraudulent affiliates.
Conversion postbacks to external ad-tech partners are batched, throttled, and sanitized by the super-app gateway to prevent timing-based side-channel leaks.

title: WICG Private State Token API: Privacy Pass Verifiable Oblivious PRF (VOPRF) Primitives and Cross-Site Anti-Abuse Tokens
summary: The WICG Private State Token API (formerly Trust Tokens) provides a privacy-preserving mechanism to convey trust and combat fraud across contexts without user tracking. Built upon the IETF Privacy Pass protocol (RFC 9576, RFC 9577, RFC 9578) using Verifiable Oblivious Pseudorandom Functions (VOPRF), issuers can cryptographically attest to client trustworthiness without linking the issuance context to the subsequent redemption context.
key_points: Private State Tokens replace linkable tracking cookies with blinded, cryptographically unforgeable tokens that convey only 2 to 3 bits of state (a categorical value chosen from 6 enum states).

Issuance and redemption utilize Privacy Pass VOPRF protocols where the client blinds a token before sending it to the issuer; the issuer signs the blinded token with private keys, allowing the client to unblind it and obtain a valid signature without the issuer observing the final token payload.
Redemption generates a signed Redemption Record (RR) that can be cached and attached via Sec-Redemption-Record HTTP headers to prove previous verification without revealing user identity.

title: Private State Token Protocol Lifecycle: Key Commitments, HTTP Sec-Headers, and Redemption Record Caching
summary: Private State Token operations are integrated into the Fetch specification. Token issuers serve cryptographic public key commitments at /.well-known/ endpoints. During issuance, clients invoke fetch() with privateToken: {operation: 'token-request'} sending Sec-Private-State-Token headers. Later, top-level origins or embedded mini-apps invoke {operation: 'token-redemption'} to produce a Redemption Record with a defined Sec-Private-State-Token-Lifetime.
key_points: Issuers maintain a /.well-known/pst-key-commitment HTTP endpoint providing cryptographic keys and expiry metadata, which user agents periodically fetch and validate.
Token issuance requests send masked tokens via the Sec-Private-State-Token request header; issuers return base64-encoded signed masked tokens via Sec-Private-State-Token response headers.
Redemption operations exchange a valid token for a Redemption Record cached in the browser's tokenStore, governed by Sec-Private-State-Token-Lifetime response headers (measured in seconds).

title: IETF Privacy Pass Standards Suite: RFC 9576 Architecture, RFC 9577 Two-Party Protocols, and RFC 9578 HTTP Authentication
summary: RFC 9576 defines the official architecture for privacy-preserving attestation, establishing roles for Clients, Issuers, Origins, and Attesters. RFC 9577 specifies the two-party token issuance protocols based on Prime-order elliptic curves (Curve25519 and P-256) and VOPRF construction (RFC 9497). RFC 9578 defines the HTTP authorization challenge and token transmission scheme (WWW-Authenticate: PrivateToken).
key_points: RFC 9576 categorizes token types into Type 1 (batched blind RSA tokens) and Type 2 (blind VOPRF tokens), ensuring that redemption is cryptographically unlinkable to issuance.
RFC 9577 standardizes cryptographic primitives for blind RSA (RSABSSA-SHA384-PSS-Zeroize) and VOPRF(P-256, SHA-256), providing zero-knowledge proofs of issuer public key consistency.
RFC 9578 standardizes the HTTP WWW-Authenticate: PrivateToken challenge-response mechanism, enabling servers to demand cryptographic anti-abuse tokens without triggering intrusive CAPTCHAs.

title: PST Security Limits: 2-Issuer Top-Level Origin Clamping, Permissions Policy Gating, and Identity Leakage Mitigations
summary: To prevent colluding origins from creating multi-bit tracking vectors by chaining token redemptions across multiple issuers, the Private State Token API enforces strict runtime limits. The user agent restricts the number of active token issuers to at most 2 per top-level origin. Operations are guarded by the Permissions-Policy: private-state-token-redemption directive with default allowlist 'self'.
key_points: Top-level origins are restricted to associating with at most 2 token issuers, preventing malicious sites from encoding user fingerprints across an arbitrary array of trust issuers.

The policy-controlled feature 'private-state-token-redemption' governs 'send-redemption-record' and 'token-redemption' operations, preventing embedded third-party iframes from redeeming tokens without top-level consent.
Redemption Records are cleared synchronously upon user data deletion (Clear-Site-Data: 'cookies', 'storage') and are partitioned by top-level site to prevent cross-site identity joining.
